title: Clinical Pathway Management for Platelet-Rich Plasma Therapy in Kellgren-Lawrence Grade I and II Knee Osteoarthritis: A Prospective, Multicenter, Double-Blind Randomized Controlled Trial.
authors: Yang S, Wang H, Liu Y, Fu F, Xu P, Li Q, Li J, Tian X, Chen G
abstract:
1. Am J Sports Med. 2026 Oct 26:3635465261486945. doi: 10.1177/03635465261486945.
 Online ahead of print.

Clinical Pathway Management for Platelet-Rich Plasma Therapy in 
Kellgren-Lawrence Grade I and II Knee Osteoarthritis: A Prospective, 
Multicenter, Double-Blind Randomized Controlled Trial.

Yang S(1)(2)(3), Wang H(2)(4)(5), Liu Y(5), Fu F(6), Xu P(7), Li Q(2)(3), Li 
J(2)(3), Tian X(1)(8)(9)(10), Chen G(2)(3).



BACKGROUND: Clinical outcomes after platelet-rich plasma (PRP) treatment for 
knee osteoarthritis are inconsistent, and some well-designed trials show no 
benefit. Whether a standardized multicomponent pathway improves outcomes 
relative to conventional PRP care is uncertain.
PURPOSE: To compare the efficacy, safety, satisfaction, and costs of a 
standardized PRP pathway versus physician-directed conventional PRP care in 
Kellgren-Lawrence grade I and II knee osteoarthritis.
STUDY DESIGN: Randomized controlled trial; Level of evidence, 1.
METHODS: At 3 hospitals, 240 patients were randomized 1:1 to a standardized PRP 
clinical pathway (PRP-CP; n = 120) or physician-directed conventional PRP care 
(PRP-C; n = 120). PRP-CP combined standardized selection, quality-controlled 
leukocyte-poor PRP, ultrasound-guided injections, staged rehabilitation, and 
systematic follow-up. Primary 12-month outcomes were visual analog scale (VAS) 
pain, Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) 
total, and International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) scores; secondary 
outcomes included achievement of the minimal clinically important difference, 
satisfaction, adverse events, and costs.
RESULTS: At 12 months, PRP-CP produced greater changes than PRP-C in VAS (mean 
difference [MD], -2.98 [95% CI, -3.64 to -2.32]), WOMAC total (MD, -8.63 [95% 
CI, -11.35 to -5.90]), and IKDC (MD, 10.25 [95% CI, 8.37 to 12.13]) scores (all 
P < .001). Achievement of the minimal clinically important difference favored 
PRP-CP at 3, 6, and 12 months for the VAS and at 6 and 12 months for the IKDC 
and WOMAC (P < .05). Satisfaction was greater with PRP-CP (odds ratio, 1.79 [95% 
CI, 1.11-2.89]; P = .017). An adverse event occurred in 17 of 115 patients in 
the PRP-CP group (14.8%) versus 36 of 113 patients in the PRP-C group (31.9%) 
(Fisher exact test: P = .003). Mean costs were CN¥15,199.9 versus CN¥14,754.4, 
respectively; the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio was CN¥66.0 per WOMAC 
point. Effects were generally consistent across centers, and blinding was 
maintained.
CONCLUSION: The standardized multicomponent pathway produced greater 12-month 
improvements in pain and function than conventional PRP care, with fewer adverse 
events. Because components were bundled and no placebo group was included, the 
trial does not establish PRP efficacy or component-specific effects.

title: Formal consensus on fast-track hip and knee arthroplasty: ESSKA/EKA, EHS and APAS recommendations for optimised recovery pathways in joint replacement surgeries.
authors: Totlis T, Kort N, Kort R, Budhiparama NC, Carulli C, Clarius M, Coden G, Gamie Z, Gomberg B, Grant A, Guenther D, Haddad FS, Kayani B, Kenanidis E, Królikowska A, Liu D, Lumban-Gaol I, Machado L, Nandi S, Pérez-Prieto D, Prill R, Smith E, Tandogan R, Tsiridis E, Beek RV
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov;34(11):4239-4255. doi: 
10.1002/ksa.70594. Epub 2026 Sep 16.

Formal consensus on fast-track hip and knee arthroplasty: ESSKA/EKA, EHS and 
APAS recommendations for optimised recovery pathways in joint replacement 
surgeries.

Totlis T(1)(2), Kort N(3), Kort R(3), Budhiparama NC(4)(5)(6), Carulli C(7), 
Clarius M(8), Coden G(9), Gamie Z(10)(11), Gomberg B(12), Grant A(9)(13), 
Guenther D(14), Haddad FS(15)(16), Kayani B(17), Kenanidis E(10)(11), 
Królikowska A(18), Liu D(19), Lumban-Gaol I(6)(20), Machado L(21)(22), Nandi 
S(23), Pérez-Prieto D(24)(25), Prill R(26), Smith E(9)(27), Tandogan R(28), 
Tsiridis E(10)(11), Beek RV(29).



PURPOSE: This international formal consensus aims to establish a unified, 
evidence-based approach to perioperative care by promoting the adoption of 
fast-track surgery or enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) protocols, 
informing healthcare professionals and administrators about optimal 
perioperative management of arthroplasty and facilitating broader 
implementation.
METHODS: A multidisciplinary panel of 106 experts contributed across a Steering 
Group (n = 22), a Rating Group (n = 35) and a Peer Review group (n = 49). The 
Steering Group developed 37 questions and corresponding statements based on the 
literature review and expert opinion. Statements were graded from A (high-level 
evidence) to D (expert opinion). An independent Rating Group evaluated each 
statement on a 1-9 Likert scale across two rounds using the Formal Consensus 
methodology. Statements were iteratively revised and finalised through consensus 
and joint discussion. The final document was assessed by an international Peer 
Review Group to ensure transnational applicability.
RESULTS: Out of 37 questions, a total of 63 statements were developed. Following 
a set of general statements outlining the principles and overall goals of 
fast-track total knee arthroplasty (TKA) and total hip arthroplasty (THA), the 
recommendations addressed and optimised the three key phases of perioperative 
care: preoperative, intraoperative and postoperative management. Of the 63 
statements, 39 were graded A or B and 24 as C or D. Mean agreement scores ranged 
from 7.7 to 8.9. Overall, 56 statements were considered appropriate with strong 
agreement and 7 with relative agreement. The Peer Review Group supported the 
overall statements, providing feedback to clarify specific recommendations and 
to highlight regional differences in implementation, which were incorporated 
into the final document.
CONCLUSIONS: This consensus endorses the adoption of structured fast-track or 
enhanced recovery programs as a patient-centred approach to perioperative care 
in total hip and knee arthroplasty. The aim is to improve the quality of care by 
reducing morbidity, optimising pain management, shortening hospital stay and 
enhancing patient satisfaction. While not intended to replace clinical 
judgement, it provides a pragmatic framework to guide decision-making, promote 
consistency and facilitate safe early mobilisation and discharge.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I.

title: Implant-Related Complications After Robotic-Assisted Versus Manual Revision Knee Arthroplasty: A Propensity-Matched Cohort Study.
authors: Mzeihem M, Rteil A, Farid Y, Martini O, Piponov H, Puri L, Amirouche F
abstract:
1. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2026 Nov 1;34(21):e3133-e3143. doi: 
10.5435/JAAOS-D-25-01589. Epub 2026 Jul 31.

Implant-Related Complications After Robotic-Assisted Versus Manual Revision Knee 
Arthroplasty: A Propensity-Matched Cohort Study.

Mzeihem M(1), Rteil A, Farid Y, Martini O, Piponov H, Puri L, Amirouche F.



INTRODUCTION: As robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty (TKA) gains traction 
in revision procedures, the urgent need to investigate its effectiveness 
compared with manual methods becomes apparent.
METHODS: Data were retrospectively obtained from the TriNetX Collaborative 
Network. Revision TKA (rKA) cases were identified using CPT codes and 
categorized as manual or robotic assisted using ICD-10 procedure codes. Cohorts 
were balanced with 1:1 propensity score matching for demographics, 
comorbidities, and revision history. Complication rates were compared across 
follow-up using chi-square analysis.
RESULTS: An initial query identified 19,088 manual and 2,709 robotic-assisted 
rKA cases. After 1:1 propensity matching, 2,010 patients remained in each group. 
Robotic rKA had significantly lower mechanical implant‑related complications at 
3 and 6 months (OR 1.67 and 1.66; P < 0.001) and lower early VTE, while PJI, 
readmission, and revision rates were not significantly different. Manual rKA 
showed higher opioid use at 0 to 3 months (OR 1.40, 95% CI, 1.14 to 1.71, P < 
0.001) and 3 to 6 months (OR 1.28, 95% CI, 1.12 to 1.47, P < 0.001) and 
throughout the 3 years of follow-up.Throughout the follow-up period, patellar 
dislocation, wound infection, non‑implant-related complications, and transfusion 
did not differ. At 1 year, manual rKA had higher instability (OR 1.59; P = 
0.001) and higher hazard of mechanical implant‑related complications (HR 1.52, 
95% CI, 1.32 to 1.75; P = 0.049). Instability, loosening, and periprosthetic 
fracture remained higher at 2 to 3 years, and revision was significantly more 
frequent at 3 years (13.5% vs. 11.4%; OR 1.22, 95% CI, 1.02 to 1.46; P = 0.03).
DISCUSSION: Robotic-assisted rKA was associated with markedly lower mechanical 
implant‑related complications across early and midterm follow-up, including 
reduced rates of instability, aseptic loosening, periprosthetic fracture, VTE, 
and lower opioid requirements. Rates of PJI, readmission, and revision were 
largely comparable, although manual rKA demonstrated a markedly higher revision 
rate by 3 years. These findings suggest that robotic assistance may improve 
implant reliability and postoperative recovery, but prospective studies and 
cost-effectiveness analyses remain necessary.

ligament (ACL). We measure stability in millimetres and celebrate isokinetic

title: Superior patient-reported clinical outcomes after patient-individual total knee arthroplasty compared with off-the-shelf robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty in valgus knee phenotypes.
authors: Tuecking LR, Savov P, Hold M, Stauss R, Windhagen H, Ettinger M
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov;34(11):4125-4132. doi: 
10.1002/ksa.70399. Epub 2026 Apr 16.

Superior patient-reported clinical outcomes after patient-individual total knee 
arthroplasty compared with off-the-shelf robotic-assisted total knee 
arthroplasty in valgus knee phenotypes.

Tuecking LR(1), Savov P(1)(2), Hold M(1), Stauss R(1)(2), Windhagen H(1), 
Ettinger M(1)(2).



PURPOSE: To compare early patient-reported clinical outcomes of 
patient-individual total knee arthroplasty (TKA) with individualized trochlear 
design versus robotic-assisted TKA using off-the-shelf implants in patients with 
valgus knee phenotypes and pronounced femoral valgus (lateral distal femoral 
angle [LDFA] < 85°) at 3 and 12 months postoperatively in a prospective matched 
case-control study.
METHODS: This prospective matched case-control study based on predefined 
anatomical criteria included 42 patients who underwent primary TKA between 
October 2021 and October 2023. Twenty-one patients received patient-individual 
posterior-stabilized implants. Twenty-one matched controls underwent 
robotic-assisted TKA with off-the-shelf implants. All procedures followed 
restricted kinematic alignment (KA) principles with valgus undercorrection. 
Primary outcomes were patient-reported scores (Forgotten Joint Score [FJS], 
Kujala Score, Oxford Knee Score [OKS] and the Western Ontario and McMaster 
Universities Arthritis Index [WOMAC]), assessed preoperatively and at 3 and 12 
months.
RESULTS: Both groups demonstrated comparable preoperative clinical status and 
comparable degrees of preoperative valgus deformity, with no significant 
differences in hip-knee-ankle angle (HKA, 185.6 ± 6.3° vs. 188.8 ± 4.1°; 
p = 0.060) or mechanical LDFA (84.0 ± 0.9° vs. 83.7 ± 1.2°; p = 0.261). At 3 and 
12 months, patient-individual total knee arthroplasty (pTKA) demonstrated 
significantly better scores across all patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) 
(p < 0.05). The largest difference was observed in the Kujala score at 12 months 
(79.5 ± 12.8 vs. 59.7 ± 19.0, p = 0.001). FJS improved more rapidly in the pTKA 
group (from 9.0 to 49.1 at 3 months, and 52.5 at 12 months) compared to 
robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty (rTKA) (26.9 and 36.0, respectively). 
One revision for suspected infection occurred in the pTKA cohort; none were 
reported after rTKA.
CONCLUSIONS: Patient-individual TKA with individualized trochlear design 
achieved superior early functional outcomes compared to robotic-assisted TKA 
with standard implants in severe valgus morphotypes. Individualized trochlear 
orientation may improve patellofemoral mechanics and facilitate faster recovery 
in patients with severe femoral valgus.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: Single-stage revision for chronic fistulized infected total knee arthroplasty achieves infection-free survival comparable to non-fistulized cases.
authors: Barbaret A, Jacquet J, Wong P, Zhu D, Collignon F, Oberle T, Lajoinie L, Ferri C, Rouizi K, Vaz G, Fernandez A, Bevilacqua S, Roche O
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov;34(11):4032-4040. doi: 
10.1002/ksa.70328. Epub 2026 Feb 6.

Single-stage revision for chronic fistulized infected total knee arthroplasty 
achieves infection-free survival comparable to non-fistulized cases.

Barbaret A(1), Jacquet J(1), Wong P(2), Zhu D(2), Collignon F(1), Oberle T(1), 
Lajoinie L(1), Ferri C(1), Rouizi K(1), Vaz G(2), Fernandez A(1), Bevilacqua 
S(3), Roche O(1).



PURPOSE: The presence of a sinus tract in chronic periprosthetic joint infection 
(PJI) has traditionally been considered a contraindication to single-stage total 
knee arthroplasty (TKA) revision. However, an increasing number of surgeons are 
now performing single-stage revisions in this context, despite limited 
comparative data. This study aimed to evaluate whether single-stage revision 
outcomes differ between fistulized (TKA/F+) and non-fistulized (TKA/F-) infected 
TKAs.
METHOD: A retrospective case-control study was conducted at a regional reference 
centre for bone and joint infections, including all patients who underwent 
single-stage TKA revision for chronic infection between January 2013 and June 
2023, with a minimum two-year follow-up. Patients were grouped according to the 
presence (TKA/F+) or absence (TKA/F-) of a sinus tract. The primary outcome was 
infection-free survival. Surgical procedures, antibiotic protocols and follow-up 
schedules were standardized across both groups. Survival analysis was performed 
using the Kaplan-Meier method and log-rank test.
RESULTS: A total of 285 patients were included: 47 TKA/F+ and 238 TKA/F-. The 
TKA/F+ group had significantly older patients, higher body mass index (BMI) and 
American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) scores, and more comorbidities. 
Polymicrobial infections were more frequent in TKA/F+ (57% vs. 22%). Despite 
these differences, infection-free survival rates were similar: 81.2% (±4.3) in 
TKA/F+ versus 83.6% (±2.2) in TKA/F-, with no statistically significant 
difference. Surgical management included extensive debridement, systematic 
sampling, gentamicin-loaded cement and local flap coverage when needed.
CONCLUSION: Single-stage revision may be effective in patients with a sinus 
tract when performed within a structured surgical and antibiotic protocol. Some 
stronger studies are needed to assess whether the presence of a sinus tract 
should not be considered an absolute contraindication. These findings support 
broader consideration of single-stage strategies in chronic TKA infections.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: An Evaluation of Precision in Implant Placement During the Early Learning Curve for the Direct Anterior Approach in Total Hip Arthroplasty.
authors: Wilke BK, Choudhury P, Baranek ME, Garner HW, Iturregui J, Stanborough RO, Sebro RA
abstract:
1. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2026 Oct 29. doi: 10.5435/JAAOS-D-24-00978. Online
ahead  of print.

An Evaluation of Precision in Implant Placement During the Early Learning Curve 
for the Direct Anterior Approach in Total Hip Arthroplasty.

Wilke BK(1), Choudhury P, Baranek ME, Garner HW, Iturregui J, Stanborough RO, 
Sebro RA.



BACKGROUND: Acquiring new skills is associated with a requisite learning curve, 
with potential for increased complications. While previous studies have 
evaluated complications associated with the learning curve for the direct 
anterior approach, no studies have evaluated whether there is a decrease in 
surgical precision during this formative period. The purpose of our study was to 
compare the precision of implant placement during a surgeon's early learning 
curve with the direct anterior (DA) approach for total hip arthroplasty (THA) 
with that of the surgeon's previous approach.
METHODS: Between 7/2012 and 3/2021, five surgeons converted from a posterior 
(PA) or anterolateral (AL) approach to a DA approach for primary THA. For each 
surgeon, initial cases using the DA approach were compared 1:1 with cases using 
the PA or AL approach before the transition. Radiographic parameters were 
recorded for each patient. Statistical analysis was conducted using the Bartlett 
test (precision) for homogeneity of variances and the F-test for pairwise 
comparisons of variances across surgical approaches.
RESULTS: A total of 618 patients were included. Across all surgeons, the DA 
approach was more precise with postoperative leg length (P = 0.003) and femoral 
offset (P = 0.009) when compared with the PA approach and more precise with leg 
length (P = 0.016) when compared with the AL approach. No loss in precision was 
observed with the DA approach compared with the PA and AL approaches for 
acetabular inclination (all P < 0.05).
CONCLUSION: The direct anterior approach demonstrated comparable or improved 
precision with implant positioning even during a surgeon's early learning curve.

title: Short-term benefits of hybrid graft in medial patellofemoral ligament reconstruction for recurrent patellar dislocation: A prospective randomized controlled trial with minimum 2-year follow-up.
authors: Zhang X, Zhai W, Wang D, Xu S, Zhou H, Guo J, Xue Z, Zhang J
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Oct 26. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70644.
Online  ahead of print.

Short-term benefits of hybrid graft in medial patellofemoral ligament 
reconstruction for recurrent patellar dislocation: A prospective randomized 
controlled trial with minimum 2-year follow-up.

Zhang X(1), Zhai W(2), Wang D(1), Xu S(1), Zhou H(1), Guo J(1), Xue Z(3), Zhang 
J(1).



PURPOSE: This study aimed to compare short-term functional and radiological 
outcomes between autograft and hybrid graft reconstruction in medial 
patellofemoral ligament (MPFL) reconstruction for recurrent patellar dislocation 
and explore reasons for differences.
METHODS: This prospective randomized controlled trial enroled 51 patients with 
recurrent patellar dislocation undergoing MPFL reconstruction between January 
2020 and January 2023. Major exclusions included severe trochlear dysplasia 
(Dejour Type B-D), open physis, patella alta, severe lower limb malalignment 
(knee valgus angle >20°, femoral anteversion >25° or external tibial torsion 
>30°) and tibial tubercle-trochlear groove (TT-TG) distance ≥20 mm. Patients 
were randomly assigned to autograft or hybrid graft groups; the hybrid graft 
comprised a semitendinosus tendon and 6-mm artificial ligament tape. The primary 
outcome was the 12-month Kujala score, prespecified for early functional 
recovery. Secondary outcomes included Kujala and International Knee 
Documentation Committee (IKDC) scores at other time points and imaging 
parameters (patellar lateral tilt [PLT] angle and patellar-trochlear groove 
[PTG] distance) preoperatively, immediately postoperatively and at final 
follow-up.
RESULTS: Forty-six patients were included in the final analysis (autograft, 
n = 22; hybrid graft, n = 24). Mean age was 19.3 years; 82.6% (38/46) were 
female. Baseline characteristics and preoperative functional scores were 
comparable between groups (all p > 0.05). Significant improvements in subjective 
knee scores were observed in both groups at 3, 6, 12 months and final follow-up 
(p < 0.05). At 3 months, mean Kujala and IKDC scores were 68.6 ± 5.2 and 
68.0 ± 6.1 in the autograft group versus 82.4 ± 4.3 and 82.9 ± 3.3 in the hybrid 
graft group (both p < 0.001). At 6 months, corresponding scores were 83.4 ± 3.6 
and 83.3 ± 3.3 versus 88.4 ± 4.6 and 88.0 ± 4.9 (both p < 0.05). No significant 
between-group differences were observed at 12 months or final follow-up (all 
p > 0.05). No significant between-group differences in PLT angle and PTG 
distance were observed immediately postoperatively or at final follow-up (all 
p > 0.05), with significant improvements from preoperative values in both groups 
(p < 0.05).
CONCLUSION: In carefully selected patients with recurrent patellar dislocation, 
MPFL reconstruction using a hybrid graft achieved satisfactory short-term 
clinical and radiographic outcomes and was associated with improved early 
functional recovery at 3 and 6 months. The hybrid graft may be a feasible option 
for MPFL reconstruction.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level II.

title: Double-level osteotomy versus high tibial osteotomy for varus malalignment of the knee: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
authors: Alkatheeri A, Ghandour M, Mobarak HA, Pierce T, Bonne S, Chalfoun AD, Jaber S, Wehbe A, Chaiban C, Ghosn A, Aoun M, Chahine M, Ollivier M
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Oct 26. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70656.
Online  ahead of print.

Double-level osteotomy versus high tibial osteotomy for varus malalignment of 
the knee: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

Alkatheeri A(1), Ghandour M(2), Mobarak HA(3)(4), Pierce T(5), Bonne S(6), 
Chalfoun AD(7), Jaber S(8), Wehbe A(7), Chaiban C(9), Ghosn A(9), Aoun M(9), 
Chahine M(10), Ollivier M(11)(12).



PURPOSE: To compare double-level osteotomy (DLO) with high tibial osteotomy 
(HTO) for varus knee malalignment across patient-reported, radiographic, 
operative and complication outcomes.
METHODS: PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science were searched to 15 May 2026 for 
comparative DLO versus HTO studies. Outcomes were pooled with a random-effects 
model as mean differences (MD) or risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals 
(CI), with absolute values for each arm. The primary outcome was joint-line 
obliquity (JLO). Sensitivity analyses (leave-one-out, one cohort per centre, 
comparable indications) were post hoc.
RESULTS: Nine observational studies (805 knees; 306 DLO, 499 HTO) were included. 
At a mean follow-up of 3 years, postoperative JLO was lower after DLO than after 
HTO (four studies; 1.6° vs. 5.9°; MD: -4.14°, 95%CI: -5.22, -3.06; I2 = 76%). 
DLO produced a lower MPTA (seven studies; 91.3° vs. 95.4°; MD: -4.10°, 95%CI: 
-5.30, -2.90), LDFA (four studies; 86.0° vs. 90.2°; MD: -4.04°, 95%CI: -4.49, 
-3.58) and mLDFA (two studies; 85.6° vs. 89.0°; MD: -3.37°, 95%CI: -4.16, 
-2.58). The hip-knee-ankle angle difference was small (five studies; MD: -0.96°, 
95%CI: -1.83, -0.09) and not robust in sensitivity analyses. No difference was 
demonstrated for joint-line convergence angle, posterior tibial slope, any KOOS 
subscale, KSS scores or time to return to sport. Operative time was longer with 
DLO (two studies; 137 vs. 91 min; MD: 42.9, 95%CI: 25.7, 60.2). Intraoperative 
hinge fracture was less frequent with DLO (three studies; 14.0% vs. 34.6%; RR: 
0.41, 95%CI: 0.23, 0.73). No nonunion was reported.
CONCLUSIONS: At 3 years, no significant difference in patient-reported or 
functional outcomes was demonstrated between DLO and HTO. DLO achieved 
correction with less JLO and fewer hinge fractures, at the cost of a longer 
operation. Because DLO was often selected for bifocal or larger deformities, the 
radiographic differences partly reflect the indication. These 
hypothesis-generating findings require prospective confirmation.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I.

title: A Translational Approach for Treatment of Posterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries: From Foundational Anatomic and Biomechanical Studies to Validated Surgical Outcomes.
authors: LaPrade RF, Tollefson LV, Engebretsen L, Kennedy NI, Chahla J, LaPrade CM, Moatshe G, DePhillipo NN, Monson JK, Bernhardson AS
abstract:
1. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2026 Oct 26. doi: 10.5435/JAAOS-D-26-00831. Online
ahead  of print.

A Translational Approach for Treatment of Posterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries: 
From Foundational Anatomic and Biomechanical Studies to Validated Surgical 
Outcomes.

LaPrade RF(1), Tollefson LV, Engebretsen L, Kennedy NI, Chahla J, LaPrade CM, 
Moatshe G, DePhillipo NN, Monson JK, Bernhardson AS.



Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) injuries were historically managed 
nonsurgically or with primary repairs, owing to limited anatomic knowledge, 
subjective diagnostic techniques, and nonvalidated reconstructions that 
frequently failed. We describe a two-decade, bench-to-bedside PCL research 
pyramid that progressively addressed these deficiencies. Foundational cadaveric 
work characterized the quantitative anatomy of the PCL, including the 
anterolateral and posteromedial bundles, yielding reproducible femoral and 
tibial osseous landmarks for tunnel placement. Robotic biomechanical testing 
established the codominant contribution of both bundles, optimal graft fixation 
angles, and the destabilizing influence of posterolateral corner injuries and 
flat tibial slope. Objective diagnostic methods, such as kneeling PCL stress 
radiography and posterior tibial translation on MRI, were validated to quantify 
laxity and detect chronic tears. These insights informed an anatomically 
grounded double-bundle reconstruction, complemented by multiligament tunnel 
convergence-avoidance strategies, evidence-based tensioning sequences, and a 
refined rehabilitation and bracing treatment protocol. Prospective outcome 
studies confirmed restoration of stability comparable to anterior cruciate 
ligament reconstructions, demonstrating how integrated translational research 
transformed treatment of this challenging injury.

title: Youth athlete development and the burden of musculoskeletal injuries: Implications of early sport specialisation.
authors: Maricot A, Tooth C, Nührenbörger C, Seil R
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov;34(11):3871-3877. doi: 
10.1002/ksa.70601. Epub 2026 Sep 16.

Youth athlete development and the burden of musculoskeletal injuries: 
Implications of early sport specialisation.

Maricot A(1), Tooth C(1)(2), Nührenbörger C(1)(3), Seil R(1)(2)(4).



Youth sport participation has increased substantially over the past two decades, 
bringing well-documented physical, social and psychological benefits. However, 
this growth has been accompanied by a rising burden of musculoskeletal injuries 
among young athletes, with prevalence rates ranging from 34% to 65%. Overuse 
injuries account for up to 50% of all youth sport injuries, while severe 
injuries such as anterior cruciate ligament reconstructions have increased 
markedly over the past two decades. Early sport specialisation (ESS), defined as 
year-round, intensive, single-sport training that excludes other sports, has 
gained traction as a perceived pathway to elite performance. However, current 
evidence does not support ESS as a reliable predictor of long-term athletic 
success. The majority of successful senior athletes were not standouts as 
youths, and early performance is a poor forecaster of adult excellence. Evidence 
examining associations between ESS and injury risk remains limited and 
methodologically inconsistent. Definitions of ESS vary substantially, 
measurement tools incompletely capture the construct, and relatively few 
high-quality empirical studies are available. More importantly, ESS may be 
better viewed as a proxy for a broader constellation of interacting exposures, 
including cumulative training load, recovery practices, biological maturation, 
variety of movement experiences and psychosocial stressors, which are more 
plausible determinants of injury risk and athlete development. Rather than 
asking whether ESS is inherently harmful, a more informative question is which 
combinations of training, developmental and environmental factors best support 
both performance progression and long-term athlete health. Until these 
mechanisms are more clearly understood, a cautious, individualised and 
evidence-informed approach to youth athlete development is warranted.

title: The mechanism of injury's role in jump landing mechanics after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.
authors: Hopper HM, Bruce-Leicht AS, Hart JM, Thompson XD
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov;34(11):4201-4209. doi: 
10.1002/ksa.70605. Epub 2026 Sep 16.

The mechanism of injury's role in jump landing mechanics after anterior cruciate 
ligament reconstruction.

Hopper HM(1), Bruce-Leicht AS(2), Hart JM(3), Thompson XD(4).



PURPOSE: The primary aim of this study is to determine if there is a difference 
in post-rehabilitation Landing Error Scoring System (LESS) score between 
patients who injured their anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) through a contact or 
noncontact mechanism of injury (MOI). The secondary aim is to determine if there 
is a difference in demographics, strength, and patient-reported outcomes (PROs) 
between patients who injured their ACL through a contact or noncontact MOI.
METHODS: Patients were included from a larger observational laboratory study if 
they had undergone a primary, isolated, uncomplicated ACLR. Patients were 
excluded if they had a history of other lower extremity surgery, concomitant 
ligament injury, surgical complications, or any neurologic disorder.
RESULTS: One hundred and twenty-nine patients were included in this study (age: 
21.4 ± 7.9, sex: 64 F/65 M, follow up: 8.1 ± 1.7 months). Ninety-one patients 
(70.5%) sustained a noncontact MOI, and 38 patients (29.5%) sustained a contact 
MOI. There was no difference in total LESS score (p = 0.930), frontal LESS score 
(p = 0.831) or sagittal LESS score (p = 0.980) between the contact and 
noncontact groups.
CONCLUSION: There was no statistically significant difference in total LESS 
score, frontal LESS score, or sagittal LESS score between contact and noncontact 
MOI. A considerable proportion of participants demonstrated multiple landing 
errors, indicating that assessment and rehabilitation of landing mechanics may 
remain relevant during late-stage rehabilitation. There was no statistically 
significant difference between mechanism of initial ACL injury and strength or 
PROs. The decision to allow a patient to return to play is multifactorial and 
should occur after modifiable risk factors, including jump landing mechanics, 
have been properly mitigated during rehabilitation.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: Osteotomies around the knee are associated with low short-term adverse event and reoperation rates: A 25-year national Hospital Episode Statistics analysis in England.
authors: Hennessy C, Rayes B, Faber BG, Murray J, Abram SGF
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov;34(11):4167-4178. doi: 
10.1002/ksa.70550. Epub 2026 Aug 26.

Osteotomies around the knee are associated with low short-term adverse event and 
reoperation rates: A 25-year national Hospital Episode Statistics analysis in 
England.

Hennessy C(1)(2), Rayes B(1), Faber BG(1)(3), Murray J(1), Abram SGF(1).



PURPOSE: Osteotomy around the knee (OAK) is an established joint-preserving 
procedure. We sought to use large-scale registry data to examine the short-term 
reoperation and adverse outcome rates after OAK.
METHODS: Data on high tibial osteotomy (HTO) and distal femoral osteotomy (DFO) 
patients were extracted from UK National Health Service Hospital Episode 
Statistics (HES). Patients <16 or >80 years and bilateral cases within <6 months 
were excluded. Reoperations and serious complications within 90 days were 
identified using International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision 
(ICD-10) and Office of Population Censuses and Surveys Classification of 
Surgical Operations and Procedures, 4th Revision (OPCS-4) codes. The primary 
outcome was reoperation rate at 90 days and 1 year; secondary outcomes were 
serious medical complications within 90 days, including pulmonary embolism (PE), 
myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI), 
acute kidney injury (AKI), urinary tract infection (UTI) and neurovascular 
injury. Logistic regression was done to estimate odds for serious complications.
RESULTS: A total of 24,947 osteotomies (18,871 HTO, 4490 DFO, 1586 doubles; 
23,371 patients) were included (mean age: 41 years; 62% male; Charlson index 0: 
80.42%). Within 90 days, 2.27% (95% confidence interval [CI] 2.08-2.47) 
underwent a reoperation, including 1.00% (95% CI 0.88-1.13) for infection. At 1 
year, 7.26% (95% CI 6.93-7.61) of patients underwent at least one reoperation, 
including 2.11% for infection (95% CI 1.92-2.30, n = 486); at 1 year, 0.38% (95% 
CI 0.31-0.47) had undergone arthroplasty. Within 90 days, 1.95% (95% CI 
1.78-2.13) experienced at least one adverse event. Specific serious complication 
rates included PE 0.39% (95% CI 0.32-0.47), MI 0.029% (95% CI 0.01-0.05), stroke 
0.029% (95% CI 0.01-0.05) and AKI 0.35% (95% CI 0.28-0.43). Higher comorbidity 
index was consistently associated with higher rates of reoperation and adverse 
events.
CONCLUSIONS: Knee osteotomy is a safe procedure performed in a predominantly 
young and healthy population, with low 90-day morbidity. Higher comorbidity 
index is the strongest predictor of serious complications. Female patients had a 
lower risk of reoperation but higher adverse event risks. These population-level 
findings will help inform consent discussions and may support future risk 
stratification.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I prospective cohort.

title: Promises and limitations of deep learning for predicting knee osteoarthritis progression from medical imaging: A systematic review.
authors: Gillani A, von Eisenhart-Rothe R, Woertler K, Hirschmann MT, Rueckert D, Hinterwimmer F
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov;34(11):4219-4234. doi: 
10.1002/ksa.70555. Epub 2026 Aug 3.

Promises and limitations of deep learning for predicting knee osteoarthritis 
progression from medical imaging: A systematic review.

Gillani A(1)(2), von Eisenhart-Rothe R(1), Woertler K(3), Hirschmann MT(4)(5), 
Rueckert D(2)(6), Hinterwimmer F(1)(2).



PURPOSE: To systematically evaluate the performance, methodological quality, and 
translational barriers of deep learning (DL) models for predicting knee 
osteoarthritis (KOA) progression from medical imaging.
METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched PubMed, Scopus, and Web of 
Science (inception to June 2026) for peer-reviewed studies applying DL to 
predict KOA progression from medical imaging. Two reviewers independently 
screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using PROBAST-AI. 
The primary outcome was area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 
(AUC). Narrative synthesis was performed due to heterogeneity in imaging 
modalities, outcome definitions, and prediction horizons.
RESULTS: From 1116 records, 33 studies (2019-2026) met the inclusion criteria, 
encompassing 50 predictive models. Sample sizes ranged from 340 to 52,981 knees 
(median: 4298). Nine progression definitions were identified and categorised as 
structural deterioration (n = 14), symptomatic worsening (n = 2), surgical 
endpoints (n = 8) or combined outcomes (n = 9). Nearly all studies (97%) used 
the Osteoarthritis Initiative dataset for training, and only 27% performed 
external validation. Surgery prediction models showed the highest descriptive 
median AUC (0.87), compared with structural (0.78) and symptomatic (0.79) 
progression models, but reflect non-disease factors including access to care. 
MRI-based models showed higher internal median AUCs (0.85) than radiograph-based 
models (0.81), but none underwent external validation. Externally validated 
models showed performance degradation (median AUC: 0.75 vs. 0.81 internal). 
Combining imaging modalities did not consistently improve predictions. However, 
studies leveraging longitudinal trajectories reported higher internal 
performance. Most studies showed low risk of bias in participant selection and 
outcome assessment, but 76% had unclear or high risk in the analysis domain.
CONCLUSIONS: DL models demonstrate proof-of-concept for predicting KOA 
progression but require substantial improvements before clinical deployment. 
Overcoming translational barriers requires standardised progression definitions 
integrating structural and symptomatic outcomes, rigorous multi-site validation, 
and models that effectively leverage multimodal and longitudinal data.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: N/A.

title: Predictive Factors for Manipulations Under Anesthesia After Total Knee Arthroplasty: An Analysis of 15,139 Cases.
authors: Iyer A, Culler M, Telang S, Palmer RC, Jones IA, Lieberman JR, Heckmann ND
abstract:
1. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2026 Nov 1;34(21):e3168-e3177. doi: 
10.5435/JAAOS-D-25-00735. Epub 2026 Jul 23.

Predictive Factors for Manipulations Under Anesthesia After Total Knee 
Arthroplasty: An Analysis of 15,139 Cases.

Iyer A(1), Culler M, Telang S, Palmer RC, Jones IA, Lieberman JR, Heckmann ND.



INTRODUCTION: Limited range of motion (ROM) and arthrofibrosis are complications 
that affect approximately 1 to 13% of patients after primary total knee 
arthroplasty (TKA). Manipulation under anesthesia (MUA) is the preferred 
treatment when failure to achieve adequate ROM in the early postoperative period 
occurs. This study aims to identify predictors for MUA that may guide surgeons 
in preoperative risk stratification.
METHODS: The Premier Healthcare Database was queried to identify patients aged 
18 years or older who underwent elective total knee arthroplasty. Patients who 
underwent manipulation under anesthesia within 90 days of index surgery were 
compared with patients who did not. Demographics, comorbidities, and medication 
usage were compared between cohorts using chi-squared and t-tests. Akaike 
information criterion and Bayesian information criterion minimization was done 
to create an optimal mixed-effects model to identify risk factors.
RESULTS: In total, 975,235 TKAs performed between 2015 and 2021 were identified. 
Of these, 1.55% (15,139) of patients required MUA. Patients in the MUA group 
were younger (62.47 ± 9.19 vs. 67.03 ± 9.24, P < 0.001) and more likely to be 
Black (15.91% vs. 8.29%, P < 0.001). Mixed-effects analysis revealed a decreased 
risk of MUA associated with perioperative dexamethasone (adjusted odds ratio 
[aOR] 0.925, 95% CI, 0.889-0.962, P < 0.001), daily prednisone usage (aOR 0.433, 
95% CI, 0.347-0.542, P < 0.001), and angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs) 
(aOR 0.882, 95% CI, 0.840-0.927, P < 0.001).
DISCUSSION: Younger age, female sex, and Black race were associated with an 
increased risk of MUA after TKA, while perioperative dexamethasone, daily 
steroids, and ARB use were protective. These findings may serve to aid surgeons 
in preoperative risk stratification.

title: Sport participation after isolated distal femoral osteotomy in young patients: High return-to-sport rates and predictive role of preoperative activity level.
authors: Lucidi GA, Adravanti FM, Rossi C, Bonaiuti M, Di Paolo S, Grassi A, Zaffagnini S
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov;34(11):4145-4155. doi: 
10.1002/ksa.70524. Epub 2026 Jul 13.

Sport participation after isolated distal femoral osteotomy in young patients: 
High return-to-sport rates and predictive role of preoperative activity level.

Lucidi GA(1)(2), Adravanti FM(1), Rossi C(1), Bonaiuti M(1), Di Paolo S(1), 
Grassi A(1)(2), Zaffagnini S(1)(2).



PURPOSE: The present study aimed to assess return to sport (RTS) rate, activity 
level and return to work (RTW) in young, physically active patients who 
underwent isolated distal femoral osteotomy (DFO) for lateral knee pain and 
valgus malalignment.
METHODS: A retrospective analysis was conducted on consecutive isolated DFO 
procedures performed at a single institution with a minimum 2-year follow-up. 
Inclusion criteria specified patients under the age of 45 who were active in 
sports 2 years prior to surgery. Data were collected regarding RTS rate, type of 
sports, sports impact level, RTW and complications. Univariate regression 
analyses were performed to identify predictors influencing RTS and the level of 
RTS.
RESULTS: Thirty-four patients (mean age 31.7 ± 9.7 years) were evaluated at a 
mean follow-up of 7.2 ± 3.8 years. The mean preoperative hip-knee-ankle (HKA) 
was 187.1 ± 3.1 with a mean achieved correction value of 7.7 ± 2.5°. The RTS 
rate was 79.4% (27/34), with a mean time to resumption of 5.4 ± 5.4 months. 
Among those returning to sports, 85.2% maintained their pre-symptom IMPACT 
level, though no patients reported an improvement in status. At the final 
follow-up, 67.7% remained active, averaging 4.5 ± 7.1 h of sports participation 
per week. Univariate regression identified the pre-symptom Tegner scale as a 
significant predictor of absolute RTS (odds ratio = 2.33, p = 0.018). Regarding 
occupational outcomes, 100% of patients returned to work at a mean of 4.4 
months, with 86.4% of active workers resuming previous or similar physical 
demands. The complication rate was 11.8% (4/34), with no clinical failures 
reported.
CONCLUSIONS: DFO performed in a young and active population results in high RTS 
rates and continuous sports participation even 7 years after surgery. Moreover, 
higher pre-symptoms Tegner scale was associated with higher odds of returning to 
sport compared to lower Tegner scale values.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV case series.

title: Better functional scores at 5 years following TKA with unrestricted kinematic alignment using medial-pivot versus ultracongruent implants.
authors: Marchetti E, Bulle L, Combes A, ReSurg, Laurendon L, Badet R
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov;34(11):4103-4112. doi: 
10.1002/ksa.70382. Epub 2026 Apr 22.

Better functional scores at 5 years following TKA with unrestricted kinematic 
alignment using medial-pivot versus ultracongruent implants.

Marchetti E(1)(2)(3), Bulle L(1), Combes A(1)(3); ReSurg(4); Laurendon 
L(1)(3)(5), Badet R(1)(3)(5).

Collaborators: Müller JH(4), Assous A(4), Saffarini M(4).



PURPOSE: The purpose was to compare patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) at 
5 years following total knee arthroplasty (TKA) using unrestricted kinematic 
alignment with ultracongruent (UC) versus cruciate-sacrificing medial pivot 
(CS-MP) and versus cruciate-retaining medial pivot (CR-MP) designs.
METHODS: This was a retrospective analysis of a consecutive cohort of 140 TKAs 
with UC (n = 44), CS-MP (n = 44) and CR-MP (n = 52). Of the initial cohort, 
three died, leaving a final cohort of 137 (UC, n = 43; CS-MP, n = 44; CR-MP, 
n = 50). Patients completed pre- and post-operative questionnaires of the Knee 
Society Score (KSS 2011) Symptoms, Satisfaction, Expectations and Function 
components, the Kujala score and the Forgotten Joint Score (FJS). Multivariable 
analyses were performed to assess the association of implant type (CR-MP, CS-MP 
and UC) with postoperative Kujala score and FJS, adjusting for patient 
characteristics (age, body mass index [BMI], sex, preoperative phenotype, 
expectations and Wiberg classification).
RESULTS: Postoperative Kujala scores were significantly better for CR-MP and 
CS-MP (80.1 ± 9.8 and 82.1 ± 9.8) compared to UC (73.3 ± 14.4; p = 0.007 and 
p < 0.001). After adjusting for patient factors, multivariable analysis revealed 
a statistically significant negative association between postoperative Kujala 
scores and UC (β = -6.270; p = 0.011). Postoperative FJS was significantly 
better for CS-MP compared to UC (88.9 ± 11.5 vs. 74.9 ± 23.4; p = 0.024). After 
adjusting for age and sex, multivariable analysis did not reveal a statistically 
significant association between postoperative FJS and UC (β = -6.58; p = n.s.).
CONCLUSION: At 5-year follow-up, TKA using unrestricted kinematic alignment with 
MP designs achieved superior functional outcomes compared to UC designs, but no 
significant difference between CS-MP and CR-MP designs.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: Inverse kinematic alignment outperforms adjusted mechanical alignment in varus TKA at 5 years.
authors: Winnock de Grave P, Roosens O, Vermue H, Luyckx T, Gunst P, Claeys K
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov;34(11):4063-4075. doi: 
10.1002/ksa.70387. Epub 2026 Apr 9.

Inverse kinematic alignment outperforms adjusted mechanical alignment in varus 
TKA at 5 years.

Winnock de Grave P(1), Roosens O(1)(2), Vermue H(1)(3), Luyckx T(1), Gunst P(1), 
Claeys K(4).



PURPOSE: Varus knee phenotypes might benefit more from patient-specific 
alignment strategies in total knee arthroplasty (TKA) since they deviate more 
from the mechanical, orthogonal planes. The aim of this study was to compare 
5-year functional outcomes following robotic-assisted TKA using inverse 
kinematic alignment (iKA) versus adjusted mechanical alignment (aMA), 
specifically in patients with preoperative varus alignment.
METHODS: In this retrospective matched cohort analysis, two groups of 45 
patients with preoperative varus alignment who received robotic-assisted TKA 
using either iKA or aMA were recruited. Patient groups were directly matched 
based on age, sex, height, weight, body mass index, preoperative hip-knee-ankle 
angle, type and severity of osteoarthritis, preoperative Oxford Knee Score (OKS) 
and EuroQol 5 Dimensions (EQ.-5D). Clinical outcomes were assessed using the 
OKS, the Forgotten Joint Score (FJS) and the Metabolic Equivalent of Task (MET) 
scale at 5-year postoperative. Radiographic and intraoperative data were 
compared.
RESULTS: Postoperative medial proximal tibial angle (MPTA) was higher in aMA 
(89.4° ± 0.8°) compared with iKA (86.7° ± 1.4°; p < 0.001), with a greater 
change of MPTA in aMA compared to iKA (-2.7° ± 1.6° vs. -0.4° ± 0.5°; 
p < 0.001). Distal medial femoral resections were larger in aMA (7.6 ± 1.1 mm) 
compared with iKA (6.4 ± 0.9 mm; p < 0.001). Patient-reported outcomes at 5 
years postoperatively favoured iKA, with higher postoperative OKS (44.2 ± 3.8 
vs. 40.2 ± 6.5; p = 0.001) and FJS (78.5 ± 19.9 vs. 59.4 ± 27.7; p = 0.001) 
compared to aMA. Similarly, the MET score was significantly higher in the iKA 
group (7.8 ± 2.1) compared with the aMA group (6.4 ± 2.5; p = 0.002).
CONCLUSIONS: In varus patients, iKA demonstrated superior 5-year functional 
outcomes compared to aMA with consistently higher OKS, FJS and MET scores. iKA 
better preserved the native tibial anatomy and medial femoral anatomy.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: A standardized surgical technique for debridement, antibiotics and implant retention improves treatment success rates in acute periprosthetic knee infection.
authors: Sánchez-Rosenberg G, Bartsch A, Morgenstern M, Kuehl R, Clauss M
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov;34(11):4041-4048. doi: 
10.1002/ksa.70350. Epub 2026 Feb 24.

A standardized surgical technique for debridement, antibiotics and implant 
retention improves treatment success rates in acute periprosthetic knee 
infection.

Sánchez-Rosenberg G(1)(2), Bartsch A(1)(2), Morgenstern M(1)(2), Kuehl R(1)(3), 
Clauss M(1)(2).



PURPOSE: Results after debridement, antibiotics and implant retention (DAIR) for 
acute periprosthetic knee joint infections (PJIs) vary widely. Although data are 
limited, surgeon expertise and surgical technique likely influence outcomes. 
Standardized DAIR performed by surgeons within a multidisciplinary team (MDT) 
dedicated to the treatment of PJI was hypothesized to improve treatment success.
METHODS: Patients undergoing DAIR for acute knee PJI at our institution were 
retrospectively identified, and the outcomes between the two temporally distinct 
cohorts were compared. Patients treated between January 2005 and May 2015 
without a standardized surgical DAIR technique or MDT support comprised the 
non-standardized cohort. The standardized cohort comprised of patients treated 
between October 2019 and October 2022 with a standardized DAIR technique and the 
involvement of an MDT. Treatment success was defined according to the Delphi 
consensus criteria.
RESULTS: After screening for eligibility and applying exclusion criteria, 26 
cases from the standardized cohort were compared with 31 from the 
non-standardized cohort. A higher successful treatment rate treatment success 
rate of 96.3% was observed in the standardized cohort, when compared to the 
80.6% success rate of the non-standardized cohort (p = 0.12). Patients in the 
standardized cohort were older (standardized 75.5 ± 11.2; non-standardized 
69.2 ± 9; p = 0.02) and had a longer median interval from time of implantation 
to DAIR (median interquartile range [IQR] standardized 2.5-13.5 years, 
non-standardized 0.4-2.8 years; p = 0.98). With respect to the preoperative 
laboratory values, no significant differences were observed, except for the 
percentage of polymorph nuclear cells in synovial fluid (standardized 86.3%, 
non-standardized 90.6%; p = 0.02). Staphylococcus aureus was the most frequently 
isolated pathogen in both cohorts (standardized [32%], non-standardized cohort 
[24.13%]; p = 0.55).
CONCLUSION: Performing DAIR using a standardized surgical technique with a 
dedicated MDT resulted in higher treatment success rates when compared to a 
non-standardized approach.

abstract:

gait kinematics.

Li Z(1)(2), Winnock de Grave P(1)(3), Van Criekinge T(1), Luyckx T(1)(3), Claeys 
K(1).



PURPOSE: To investigate the impact of static native tibial alignment in total 
knee arthroplasty (TKA) on whole-body postoperative gait biomechanics, comparing 
adjusted mechanical alignment (aMA) and inverse kinematic alignment (iKA).
METHODS: Thirty patients undergoing primary TKA were included: 15 in the aMA 
group (17 knees) and 15 in the iKA group (19 knees), assessed 2 years 
post-surgery. A healthy control group of 15 participants, matched for age, sex 
and body mass index (BMI), was included. Postoperative spatiotemporal and 
kinematic gait parameters were measured using 3D motion capture during gait.
RESULTS: The aMA group demonstrated persistent knee flexion around midstance 
during the stance phase (p = 0.002, >10.00°), reduced knee flexion at swing 
onset (p = 0.011, -12.00°), and decreased ankle plantarflexion (p = 0.002, 
-8.00°). Additionally, the aMA group showed reduced hip extension (p < 0.001), 
increased anterior pelvic tilt (p < 0.001), exaggerated thorax flexion 
(p = 0.003) and altered elbow motion (p < 0.015). In contrast, the iKA group 
exhibited gait patterns more closely resembling healthy controls, with a greater 
range of motion (ROM) at the hip, knee and ankle, improved ankle and foot 
progression angles, and no differences in thorax posture or elbow angles 
compared to controls.

biomechanics and suggest that subtle modifications to the knee joint line may 
contribute to widespread kinematic adaptations. Preserving static native tibial 
alignment through personalised surgical strategies may, therefore, enhance 
functional outcomes following TKA.

rotatory instability after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction and lateral 
meniscus repair.

T(4), Amemiya M(3), Yoshihara A(1), Koga H(1).



PURPOSE: This study aimed to examine the effects of lateral meniscus (LM) 
centralization on anterolateral rotational stability in patients with anterior 
cruciate ligament (ACL) and LM injuries. The hypothesis was that performing LM 
repair and centralization on knees with LM lesions would control anterolateral 
rotatory instability (ALRI).
METHODS: Twenty patients with ACL and LM injuries were enroled. Tibial 
acceleration in the pivot shift was quantified using a triaxial accelerometer at 
each preoperative and intraoperative time point (after ACL reconstruction 
(ACLR), LM repair and centralization) of double-bundle ACLR. Pivot shift was 
assessed with the ACL graft tension provisionally fixed under two conditions 
that both the anteromedial bundle (AMB) and posterolateral bundle (PLB) grafts 
were temporarily fixed at 5 N each (A5P5) and at 10 N each (A10P10). The 
Kruskal-Wallis test was used to compare the tibial accelerations between each 
time points, and the Steel-Dwass test with Bonferroni correction was used for 
multiple comparisons. Also, patient factors associated with the results of a 
higher-grade pivot shift compared to the healthy side after ACLR and LM repair 
were determined in a two-group comparison.
RESULTS: Pivot shift acceleration was significantly decreased after ACLR (PreOP 
[8.3 ± 2.1 m/s2] vs. ACLR [5.1 ± 2.1 m/s2] in A5P5, p < 0.01 and 
[4.6 ± 1.5 m/s2] in A10P10, p < 0.01). However, the subsequent LM repair did not 
significantly reduce the pivot shift (ACLR [5.1 ± 2.1 m/s2] vs. LM repair 
[4.0 ± 0.9 m/s2] in A5P5, p = 0.09 and ACLR [4.5 ± 1.5 m/s2] vs. LM repair 
[3.5 ± 1.0 m/s2] in A10P10, p = 0.10). Additional centralization significantly 
controlled the residual pivot shift in most cases (ACLR [5.1 ± 2.1 m/s2] vs. 
Centralization [2.9 ± 1.0 m/s2] in A5P5, p < 0.01 and ACLR [4.5 ± 1.5 m/s2] vs. 
Centralization [2.8 ± 0.8 m/s2] in A10P10, p < 0.01).

ACLR and LM repair, adding LM centralization further controlled ALRI in a 
relatively minimally invasive procedure.

title: Implant Choice Impacts Initial Tibial Component Micromotion in Total Ankle Replacement: A Biomechanical Analysis.
authors: Henry JK, Hoffman J, Villar R, Lu K, Kim S, Steineman BD, Demetracopoulos C
abstract:
1. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2026 Oct 29. doi: 10.2106/JBJS.26.00733. Online ahead of
 print.

Implant Choice Impacts Initial Tibial Component Micromotion in Total Ankle 
Replacement: A Biomechanical Analysis.

Henry JK(1), Hoffman J(2), Villar R(3), Lu K(1)(3), Kim S(2), Steineman BD(2), 
Demetracopoulos C(1).



BACKGROUND: Total ankle replacements (TARs) have a risk of early mechanical 
failure. Clinical studies have shown that implants with more robust tibial 
fixation-i.e., stemmed designs-have a lower early mechanical failure risk. We 
aimed to compare the micromotion between 2 tibial components with different 
fixation features, using a cadaveric robotic gait simulator. We hypothesized 
that more robust fixation accommodates loads more effectively, resulting in less 
micromotion at the bone-implant interface for stemmed tibial implants when 
compared to low-profile tibial implants.
METHODS: Specimens from 10 cadaveric matched pairs (from 6 men and 4 women, age: 
48 ± 11 years) were implanted with either a low-profile or stemmed TAR. 
Post-TAR, gait was simulated using a validated 6-degrees-of-freedom robot. A 
digital image correlation camera system captured the relative motion between the 
tibial bone and the implant via surface markers. Implant micromotion was 
calculated by performing rigid-body transformations on segmented geometries of 
the tibia and implant derived from computed tomography imaging. Peak and mean 
micromotion were defined as the maximum and mean nodal displacement, 
respectively, on the implant surface across all time points in stance. Wilcoxon 
signed-rank tests compared micromotion of stemmed and low-profile implants 
between matched pairs.
RESULTS: On average, peak and mean micromotion values were greater for 
low-profile implants by 150 µm (95% confidence interval [CI]: 98 to 203 µm) and 
30 µm (95% CI: 9 to 52 µm), respectively, compared with the matched stemmed 
implants (p < 0.001 for both). Peak micromotion of low-profile implants 
typically occurred at the posterior aspect of the implant. In contrast, stemmed 
implants demonstrated a more evenly distributed pattern with peak micromotion 
located at the tip of the stem.
CONCLUSIONS: This study identified significantly greater time-zero micromotion 
of low-profile tibial implants compared with stemmed implants. The micromotion 
distribution suggests that the stemmed implants were further compressed into 
bone, whereas the low-profile implants demonstrated a rocking motion. Our data 
support the notion that early mechanical failures of low-profile tibial implants 
may be due to excessive early micromotion.

complete description of levels of evidence.

title: Delayed return to sport after fat pad debridement: A surgical effect or a load-tolerance signal?
authors: Han X, Yang M
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Oct 28. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70663.
Online  ahead of print.

Delayed return to sport after fat pad debridement: A surgical effect or a 
load-tolerance signal?

Han X(1), Yang M(2).



This Letter responds to the meta‑analysis entitled 'Fat pad debridement prolongs 
return-to-sport: A meta-analysis and meta-regression of surgical interventions 
for chronic patellar tendinopathy' by Jolly et al., which examined surgical 
interventions for chronic patellar tendinopathy. We contend that the observed 
delay should not be attributed solely to the surgical procedure. Fat pad 
debridement may serve as a marker of a more irritable anterior-knee pain 
phenotype, given that fat pad pathology frequently coexists with impingement, 
fibrosis and peritendinous irritation. Furthermore, time to return to sport 
(RTS) is an incomplete recovery surrogate; meaningful restoration depends on 
rebuilding tendon load tolerance rather than meeting a single chronological 
milestone. We therefore advise interpreting the association as a composite 
signal of procedural, phenotypic and rehabilitative factors. Future prospective 
studies should document preoperative fat pad status, extent of debridement and 
criterion-based RTS progression, so as to determine whether fat pad preservation 
truly accelerates recovery or whether delayed RTS simply identifies athletes 
needing more individualized load management.

title: Varying Lateral Extra-articular Tenodesis Femoral Fixation Points and Fixation Flexion Angles Do Not Affect ACL Graft Force and Tibiofemoral Motion After ACL Reconstruction.
authors: Kruckeberg BM, Brady AW, Cinque ME, Sidrak JP, Kanakamedala AC, Hackett TR, Vidal AF, Godin JA
abstract:

Varying Lateral Extra-articular Tenodesis Femoral Fixation Points and Fixation 
Flexion Angles Do Not Affect ACL Graft Force and Tibiofemoral Motion After ACL 
Reconstruction.

Kruckeberg BM(1)(2), Brady AW(1), Cinque ME(1)(2), Sidrak JP(1), Kanakamedala 
AC(1)(2), Hackett TR(1)(2), Vidal AF(1)(2), Godin JA(1)(2).



BACKGROUND: The addition of lateral extra-articular tenodesis (LET) to anterior 
cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction (ACLR) has been shown to reduce 
rotational laxity and improve graft survivorship. Despite the increased 
utilization of LET with ACLR, there remains a lack of consensus on the ideal 
location of the femoral attachment site of LET.
PURPOSE: To compare ACL graft force and tibiofemoral motion in cadaveric 
specimens undergoing ACLR with the addition of LET at varying fixation angles 
and fixation points.
STUDY DESIGN: Controlled laboratory study.
METHODS: A total of 10 fresh-frozen cadaveric knees were tested in 6 conditions, 
including LET fixation at 2 anatomic locations. Location 1 was defined as 8 mm 
proximal and 4 to 5 mm posterior to the lateral femoral epicondyle, at the 
insertion of the anterolateral ligament. Location 2 was defined as 31 mm 
proximal to the lateral femoral epicondyle, at the insertion of the distal 
Kaplan fibers. The testing conditions were as follows: (1) native; (2) ACLR; (3) 
ACLR + LET at location 1, fixed at 30°; (4) ACLR + LET at location 2, fixed at 
30°; (5) ACLR + LET at location 1, fixed at 60°; and (6) ACLR + LET at location 
2, fixed at 60°. Specimens were mounted on a 6 degrees of freedom robotic system 
to assess tibial internal rotation and anterior tibial translation at 0°, 30°, 
60°, and 90° of knee flexion. A load cell was utilized to assess ACL graft 
force.
RESULTS: There were no differences between the 4 LET states in any outcome. In 
internal rotation, the addition of LET demonstrated reductions in ACL graft 
force in all 4 configurations, ranging from -14.9 N (14%) to -19.5 N (20%) at 
0°, -19.7 N (51%) to -21.4 N (55%) at 30°, and -3.9 N (30%) to -4.6 N (35%) at 
60° (all P < .05). The addition of LET also demonstrated reductions in internal 
rotation range of motion in all 4 configurations, ranging from -1.86° (15%) to 
-2.45° (19%) at 0°, -4.87° (18%) to -5.75° (20%) at 30°, and -4.70° (19%) to 
-5.92° (23%) at 60° (all P < .05).
CONCLUSION: Variations in LET fixation location and fixation flexion angle did 
not alter its effect on ACL graft force reduction or tibiofemoral motion in the 
cadaveric knee. The addition of LET had a protective effect on the ACL graft in 
internal rotation while demonstrating overconstraint compared to the native 
knee.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The findings suggest that surgeons may have flexibility in 
selecting the femoral fixation location and knee flexion angle for LET without 
substantially altering its biomechanical effect on ACL graft loading or 
tibiofemoral kinematics. However, because LET reduced internal rotation beyond 
the native state, care should be taken to avoid excessive constraint when 
performing the procedure.

abstract:

Contact injury mechanism is independently associated with greater Anterior 
Cruciate Ligament Injury Severity Scale severity in patients undergoing primary 
anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.

Malhamé ZM(1), Hardy A(2), Bouché PA(3), Santoli A(1), Miele A(2), Seil R(4), 
Pioger C(1)(5).



PURPOSE: To determine whether injury mechanism and sport category were 
independently associated with overall structural injury severity after 
sport-related primary anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture, as quantified by 
the Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Severity Scale (ACLISS).
METHODS: This retrospective analysis of prospectively collected data included 
consecutive patients undergoing primary ACL reconstruction between November 2022 
and November 2024. Eligible patients had sustained a complete primary ACL 
rupture during sport, undergone magnetic resonance imaging within 8 weeks of 
injury and had complete imaging and arthroscopic documentation. Injury mechanism 
was classified as contact or non-contact, and sports as pivoting-contact, 
pivoting-non-contact or non-pivoting. Associations with severity grade were 
assessed using proportional-odds ordinal logistic regression adjusted for age, 
sex, body mass index and injury-to-surgery interval. Models evaluated injury 
mechanism, sport category and both exposures simultaneously. The continuous 
score was examined in sensitivity analyses.
RESULTS: Among 482 patients, 175 (36.3%) sustained contact injuries and 307 
(63.7%) sustained non-contact injuries. Contact injuries had higher ACLISS mean 
scores than non-contact injuries (4.6 vs. 3.8; p < 0.001) and were more 
frequently classified in higher severity grades. In the fully adjusted model, 
contact injury remained independently associated with greater severity (odds 
ratio, 2.68; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.68-4.27; p < 0.001), whereas sport 
category was no longer associated with severity. Adding injury mechanism 
improved model fit, whereas adding sport category to a model already containing 
injury mechanism did not. Continuous-score analysis confirmed the principal 
finding (adjusted mean difference, 0.60 points; 95% CI, 0.29-0.91; p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: Among patients undergoing primary ACL reconstruction after a 
sport-related ACL rupture, contact injury mechanism was independently associated 
with greater structural injury severity. This association persisted after 
adjustment for sport category, whereas the association with sport category was 
attenuated. Injury mechanism should therefore be documented when characterizing 
injury severity.

title: Longitudinal Serum Biomarker Profiles of Inflammation and Cartilage Matrix Metabolism During the First Year After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction.
authors: Lemus SA, Spang JT, Longobardi L, Davis-Wilson HC, Creighton RA, Loeser RF, Kamath GM, Schwartz TA, Golightly Y, Nelson AE, Pietrosimone B
abstract:

Longitudinal Serum Biomarker Profiles of Inflammation and Cartilage Matrix 
Metabolism During the First Year After Anterior Cruciate Ligament 
Reconstruction.

Lemus SA(1), Spang JT(2)(3), Longobardi L(4), Davis-Wilson HC(5), Creighton 
RA(2), Loeser RF(4), Kamath GM(2), Schwartz TA(1)(4)(6), Golightly Y(4)(7), 
Nelson AE(4), Pietrosimone B(1).



BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury initiates biological 
processes linked to joint tissue degeneration. The longitudinal time course of 
serum biomarkers reflecting inflammation and cartilage metabolism after ACL 
reconstruction (ACLR), particularly in comparison with uninjured controls, has 
not been characterized across the first postoperative year.
HYPOTHESIS: Inflammatory (monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 [MCP-1]) and 
degradative (matrix metalloproteinase-3 [MMP-3]) biomarker concentrations would 
be elevated pre-ACLR and decrease over time, whereas cartilage turnover 
biomarker concentrations (cartilage oligomeric matrix protein [COMP] and type II 
collagen degradation-to-synthesis ratio [C2C:CPII]) would increase 
postoperatively. Also, pre-ACLR biomarker concentrations would be associated 
with concentrations at 6 and 12 months post-ACLR.
STUDY DESIGN: Cohort study; Level of evidence, 2.
METHODS: A total of 33 individuals with ACL injuries (52% female; mean age, 20.8 
± 2.4 years) were evaluated pre-ACLR and at 6 and 12 months post-ACLR. A total 
of 33 matched uninjured controls were included. Serum concentrations of MCP-1, 
MMP-3, COMP, and C2C:CPII were assessed using enzyme-linked immunosorbent 
assays. Linear mixed-effects models with model-based contrasts were used to 
evaluate differences across groups and time points. ACLR-only linear 
mixed-effects regression models were used to assess associations between 
pre-ACLR and follow-up biomarker concentrations. Exploratory post hoc models 
evaluated differences by concomitant injury status.
RESULTS: MCP-1 was elevated in individuals with ACL injuries compared with 
controls at all ACLR time points (all Padj < .001), with no change across ACLR 
time points. MMP-3 increased from pre-ACLR to 6 months post-ACLR (Padj < .001) 
but did not differ from controls at any time point. COMP was consistently 
greater in individuals with ACL injuries than in controls at all time points 
(all Padj≤ .021), with no changes across ACLR time points. C2C:CPII was greater 
at 12 months post-ACLR than at pre-ACLR and 6 months post-ACLR (both Padj < 
.001) and than in uninjured controls (Padj = .001). Pre-ACLR MCP-1, MMP-3, and 
COMP concentrations were associated with concentrations at both 6 and 12 months 
post-ACLR (all P≤ .006), whereas C2C:CPII was associated only with 12-month 
concentrations (P = .018).
CONCLUSION: Inflammatory and cartilage-related biomarkers remain altered 
throughout the first year after ACLR, suggesting that the biological response is 
not fully resolved by reconstruction and standard rehabilitation but extends 
beyond the early postoperative period.

authors: Rüter ML, Kösters C, den Toom DA
abstract:

focal (osteo-)chondral lesions of the distal femur.

Rüter ML(1), Kösters C(2), den Toom DA(2).



OBJECTIVES: Patient-specific mini-metal implants may represent a treatment 
option for middle-aged patients with focal (osteo-)chondral lesions of the 
distal femur when biological repair has failed or when other individual risk 
factors make biological repair unlikely to succeed. Both single-implant 
approaches for one- and dual-implant approaches for two separate lesions in the 
same knee were investigated. This study evaluates the clinical performance of 
these implants for one or two lesions in one knee.
METHODS: This retrospective single-center study was conducted using 
prospectively collected data of consecutive patients treated with one or two 
implants (Episealer Implant) with a mean follow-up of 38 months. The Knee Injury 
and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS), visual analog scale (VAS) for pain, 
adverse events, and conversions to unicompartmental or total knee arthroplasty 
were assessed.

pain score compared to the preoperative values were observed in both groups (one 
implant n = 45; two implants n = 48; all p < 0.001). KOOS symptoms improved from 
48.7 ± 17.9 to 74.3 ± 21.6 in the one-implant group and from 44.7 ± 15.0 to 66.0 
± 24.8 in the two-implant group. Similar improvements were observed across all 
remaining KOOS subscales. The comparison between the two groups revealed

according to Kaplan-Meier analysis was 88.1% for the one-implant group (number 
at risk = 21) and 83.4% for the two-implant group (number at risk = 27) after 60 
months.

treatment option for middle-aged patients when biological repair is not 
feasible. Within the limitations of this study, the findings suggest that this 
approach can be considered for patients with one as well as patients with two 
(osteo-)chondral lesions. An acceptable implant survival was observed, 
regardless of lesion count.

title: The Basic Science of Large Language Models in Orthopaedic Surgery.
authors: Dang ABC, Dang ABC
abstract:

The Basic Science of Large Language Models in Orthopaedic Surgery.

Dang ABC(1), Dang ABC.



Orthopaedic surgeons routinely consult search engines, journals, and curated 
websites to stay current on orthopaedic knowledge. The emergence of large 
language models, such as OpenAI ChatGPT and Google MedGemma, is changing the way 
we search for information and how residents learn. Although many orthopaedic 
surgeons are users of artificial intelligence (AI), most are uncertain about how 
these tools actually work and why they sometimes give impressively accurate 
explanations alongside glaring factual errors and fabricated citations. This 
review provides an overview of the underlying preclinical studies behind large 
language models at the level of detail needed to empower orthopaedic surgeons 
with the knowledge needed to critically evaluate AI outputs, design future 
research projects, and effectively incorporate AI tools into clinical practice 
and resident education. Through clinical examples including a Schatzker VI 
tibial plateau fracture and an L4 pedicle screw sizing question, we illustrate 
two distinct classes of AI failure-retrieval failures and reasoning failures-and 
demonstrate how understanding the preclinical studies behind these errors equips 
surgeons to evaluate any AI tool regardless of where or how it runs.

PURPOSE: The aim of this study was to evaluate the biomechanical consequences of 
performing an anteromedializing tibial tubercle osteotomy on a cadaveric knee 
model with increased femoral anteversion.
METHODS: A controlled biomechanical study was performed on 16 human cadaveric 
knees. Intra-articular pressures were measured under four conditions. The first 
group was the native knee (n = 16). Subsequently, the sample was divided into 
two equal groups: a group in which 30 degrees of internal femoral rotation was 
experimentally induced (n = 8), and a group in which a Fulkerson osteotomy was 
performed (n = 8). Finally, the group in which an internal rotation of 30 
degrees was experimentally induced underwent a Fulkerson osteotomy (n = 8). 
Measurements were obtained at 0°, 30°, 60° and 90° of knee flexion under a 
simulated weight-bearing squat condition using a 1000 N ground reaction force 
combined with independent quadriceps (218 N) and hamstring (80 N) loading. 
Patellofemoral and tibiofemoral compartments were analysed using intra-articular 
pressure sensors.
RESULTS: Compared with the native knee, internal femoral rotation significantly 
increased lateral patellofemoral pressure (1.220 ± 0.016 vs. 1.342 ± 0.032 MPa 
at 30° of flexion; p = 0.05) and lateral tibiofemoral pressure (1.110 ± 0.020 
vs. 1.489 ± 0.054 MPa at 90° of flexion; p = 0.004). The anteromedialization of 
the tibial tubercle partially reversed those changes. However, the technique 
failed to restore the pressure distribution to native values (all p < 0.05).
CONCLUSION: Our findings indicate that while anteromedialization of the tibial 
tubercle partially mitigates the biomechanical alterations induced by increased 
internal femoral torsion, it does not fully restore native joint pressure 
distribution. These findings suggest that isolated distal realignment may be 
insufficient in the presence of significant rotational deformity and that 
surgical strategies should also address proximal rotational abnormalities to 
optimise joint loading.

title: Restoring the coronal plane alignment of the knee (CPAK) phenotype does not consistently improve patient-reported outcomes after primary total knee arthroplasty: A systematic review.
authors: Hajiaghajani S, Poursalehian M, Salmannezhad A, Culler MW, Yun AG, Heckmann ND
abstract:

10.1002/ksa.70403. Epub 2026 Apr 16.

Restoring the coronal plane alignment of the knee (CPAK) phenotype does not 
consistently improve patient-reported outcomes after primary total knee 
arthroplasty: A systematic review.

Hajiaghajani S(1), Poursalehian M(1), Salmannezhad A(1), Culler MW(2), Yun 
AG(2), Heckmann ND(2).



PURPOSE: To evaluate restoring knee preoperative coronal plane alignment of the 
knee (CPAK) phenotype, or joint line obliquity (JLO) and arithmetic 
hip-knee-ankle angle (aHKA), is associated with superior patient-reported 
outcome measures (PROMs) after primary total knee arthroplasty (TKA).
METHODS: A systematic review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 
guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and Embase were searched from January 
2020 to February 2026. Eligible studies included adults undergoing primary TKA 
who reported validated PROMs, categorized restoration of CPAK phenotype, JLO or 
aHKA. Two reviewers independently screened, extracted and checked data. Due to 
heterogeneity in alignment strategies, definitions of restoration and outcome 
reporting, results were synthesized narratively.
RESULTS: Thirteen studies met the inclusion criteria, comprising 1 randomized 
controlled trial, 1 prospective registry-based study and 11 retrospective 
cohorts. Follow-up durations ranged from 1 to 5 years. Across studies, restoring 
the preoperative CPAK phenotype or its coronal components was not consistently 
linked with higher PROMs. Most studies found comparable PROMs regardless of CPAK 
phenotypes, JLO and aHKA restoration. Studies showing superior PROMs in 
restoration subgroups were limited, with small effect sizes and substantial 
heterogeneity. Evidence was limited by the retrospective design and the small 
sample size, particularly for valgus and uncommon phenotypes.
CONCLUSIONS: The current evidence does not demonstrate a consistent association 
between the CPAK phenotype, JLO, aHKA restoration and improved PROMs after 
primary TKA.

title: Joint line obliquity disruption negatively affects mid-term patient-reported outcomes following total knee arthroplasty.
authors: Pflüger P, Pedrazzini A, Fischer L, Jud L, Vlachopoulos L, Fucentese SF
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov;34(11):4093-4102. doi: 
10.1002/ksa.70389. Epub 2026 Apr 6.

Joint line obliquity disruption negatively affects mid-term patient-reported 
outcomes following total knee arthroplasty.

Pflüger P(1), Pedrazzini A(1), Fischer L(1), Jud L(1), Vlachopoulos L(1), 
Fucentese SF(1).



PURPOSE: The influence of change in coronal alignment on clinical outcomes 
following total knee arthroplasty (TKA) remains unclear. The Coronal Plane 
Alignment of the Knee (CPAK) classification can be broken up into arithmetic 
hip-knee-ankle (aHKA) angle and joint line obliquity (JLO) components, 
potentially identifying distinct failure mechanisms. This study investigated the 
influence of change in the magnitude and surgical accuracy of CPAK on 
patient-reported mid-term outcomes and the risk of aseptic revision.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study included 216 patients (234 TKAs, median 
age 66 years, 65.3% women) undergoing patient-specific instrumentation in TKA 
with a minimum follow-up of 5 years. The change in CPAK was divided into aHKA 
and JLO components. Surgical accuracy was defined as deviation from the planned 
HKA angle. The primary outcome was the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities 
Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC). A secondary outcome was aseptic revision of TKA. 
Multi-stage method robust regression and logistic regression models were used, 
after adjustment for preoperative WOMAC scores and reintervention.
RESULTS: The median WOMAC score improved from 50 (interquartile range [IQR] 
24.3) preoperatively to 11 (IQR 19) postoperatively. Our analysis of change in 
CPAK components revealed JLO disruption as the primary predictor associated with 
inferior outcomes, with each step change associated with worse WOMAC scores 
(β = 3.98, p = 0.02) and increased revision risk (odds ratio = 3.15, p = 0.04). 
In contrast, change in aHKA was not associated with either outcome.
CONCLUSION: Within the CPAK framework, JLO disruption emerged as the primary 
predictor of patient-reported inferior outcomes and risk of aseptic revision 
following TKA. Our current findings highlight the importance of preserving 
native JLO within personalized alignment strategies. Future prospective studies 
are needed to establish the acceptable degree of JLO change that maintains 
optimal joint kinematics and patient satisfaction.

title: Contemporary patellofemoral arthroplasty is associated with lower revision rates compared with the previous decade: A meta-analysis using revisions per 100 component-years.
authors: Clar C, Budin M, Rasic L, Leithner A, Linden JV, Sadoghi P
abstract:
