10.1002/ksa.70381. Epub 2026 Mar 10.

Contemporary patellofemoral arthroplasty is associated with lower revision rates 
compared with the previous decade: A meta-analysis using revisions per 100 
component-years.

Clar C(1), Budin M(1), Rasic L(1), Leithner A(1), Linden JV(1), Sadoghi P(1).



PURPOSE: The aim of this study was to assess global data on patellofemoral 
arthroplasty (PFA) survival a decade after a prior investigation by Reihs et al. 
using the same endpoints and data sources, aiming to quantify potential changes 
in implant survival over this period. The hypothesis was that the pooled 
revision rate of contemporary PFA, quantified as revisions per 100 
component-years (CY), would be lower than prior decade estimates derived from 
identical methodology and registry sources.
METHODS: A systematic search in Embase, MEDLINE and CENTRAL through October 2025 
using a predefined search strategy was conducted using Ovid. Two reviewers 
screened and extracted data. The primary effect measure was revisions per 100 
CY. Pooled estimates were obtained with fixed- and DerSimonian-Laird 
random-effects. Risk of bias was assessed with ROBINS-I. National arthroplasty 
registries meeting EAR/EUPHORIC Type A.1.1.1.1. criteria were analyzed.
RESULTS: Fifteen primary studies were included, with most series using 
contemporary onlay designs. Per-study rates ranged from 0.355 to 3.400/100 CY. 
The pooled revision rate was 1.59/100 CY (95% confidence interval 
[CI] = 1.24-2.04) with random effects, corresponding to a 10-year revision rate 
of 15.9%, representing an absolute improvement of 6.3% in survivorship compared 
to the benchmark analysis by Reihs et al. heterogeneity was moderate 
(I2 = 52.7%). ROBINS-I indicated predominantly critical risk of bias. Registry 
synthesis (NJR, NZJR, AOANJRR, 117.524 CY) yielded 1.85/100 CY (95% 
CI = 1.775-1.931), corresponding to a 10-year revision rate of 18.5% (95% 
CI = 17.75-19.3) and an improvement of 0.4%-8.5% in the last decade if compared 
to Reihs et al. CONCLUSIONS: This meta-analysis demonstrates that modern PFA has 
a more favourable survivorship profile over the past decade, particularly with 
onlay designs. Proper patient selection and registry-based surveillance remain 
key to further optimization.

title: A fixed 2 mm adjustment for worn distal femoral cartilage when the cartilage of the unworn compartment is ≥3 mm does not negatively affect outcome scores after kinematically aligned total knee arthroplasty.
authors: Nedopil AJ, Mamidi D, Howell SM, Hull ML
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov;34(11):4023-4031. doi: 
10.1002/ksa.70320. Epub 2026 Feb 16.

A fixed 2 mm adjustment for worn distal femoral cartilage when the cartilage of 
the unworn compartment is ≥3 mm does not negatively affect outcome scores after 
kinematically aligned total knee arthroplasty.

Nedopil AJ(1)(2), Mamidi D(3), Howell SM(4), Hull ML(2)(4)(5)(6).



PURPOSE: A goal of kinematic alignment (KA) total knee arthroplasty (TKA) is to 
align the femoral component to restore the distal and posterior femoral joint 
lines to prearthritic. To restore the joint line on the worn distal condyle, the 
resection thickness is adjusted by 2 mm for cartilage loss based on the reported 
average cartilage thickness on magnetic resonance imaging. It remains unclear 
whether a 2 mm fixed adjustment is ideal for all patients, especially those with 
thicker cartilage. This study examined whether a 2 mm fixed adjustment in 
patients with cartilage thickness ≥3.0 mm negatively affects the Forgotten Joint 
Score (FJS), Oxford Knee Score (OKS) and Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome 
Score for Joint Replacement (KOOS JR) compared to those with cartilage thickness 
<3.0 mm.
METHODS: In 96 KA TKAs with preoperative varus (85%) and valgus (15%) 
deformities, cartilage thickness was measured using a calibrated photographic 
method on a medial-lateral bisection of the unworn distal femoral condyle. At 1 
year after surgery, equivalence was assessed in FJS, OKS and KOOS JR between 
patients with cartilage thickness ≥3.0 mm and those with <3.0 mm.
RESULTS: The overall average cartilage thickness was 2.8 ± 0.6 mm (range, 
1.6-5.0 mm), with 41% having a cartilage thickness ≥3.0 mm. The mean FJS was 78 
versus 74 points for those with <3.0 and ≥3.0 mm cartilage, and these results 
were statistically equivalent (p = 0.0150). Similarly, mean OKS scores of 42 
versus 41 points (p = 0.0071), and KOOS JR scores of 80 versus 81 points, were 
statistically equivalent (p < 0.0001).
CONCLUSION: Although a large percentage of patients had unworn cartilage 
thickness ≥3 mm, outcome scores were comparble to patients with thickness <3 mm. 
Hence, surgeons can use a 2 mm fixed adjustment for cartilage loss, even when 
the cartilage thickness exceeds 3 mm, with a range up to 5.0 mm, 
without negatively affecting the FJS, OKS or KOOS JR.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: Rethinking early arthrogenic muscle inhibition after total knee arthroplasty.
authors: Qu X, Sun G, Chen B
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Oct 30. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70664.
Online  ahead of print.

Rethinking early arthrogenic muscle inhibition after total knee arthroplasty.

Qu X(1), Sun G(1), Chen B(1).



We read with interest the recent article by Barrera Uso et al. on early 
arthrogenic muscle inhibition (AMI) after total knee arthroplasty (TKA). The 
study provides clinically relevant evidence that AMI at 30 days strongly 
predicts persistence at 60 days. We suggest, however, that this finding should 
be interpreted as a prognostic association rather than evidence that 30-day AMI 
is the dominant biological determinant of subsequent inhibition. We also discuss 
the timing of postoperative assessment, noting that evaluation at 30 days is 
appropriate for studying persistence but less informative regarding the initial 
pathophysiological development of AMI. The Scientific Anterior Cruciate Ligament 
Network International (SANTI) classification has demonstrated excellent 
reliability in anterior cruciate ligament populations, although its 
generalizability to TKA remains to be specifically established. Finally, the 
absence of objective functional and patient-reported outcomes limits 
interpretation of the clinical significance of persistent AMI. Overall, the 
study identifies an important clinical phenotype and useful prognostic markers 
while leaving the underlying mechanisms of persistence to be further clarified.

title: Rethinking the functional relevance of posterolateral tibial plateau fractures in anterior cruciate ligament injury.
authors: Qu X, Tang X, Yang D, Chen B
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Oct 28. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70662.
Online  ahead of print.

Rethinking the functional relevance of posterolateral tibial plateau fractures 
in anterior cruciate ligament injury.

Qu X(1), Tang X(1), Yang D(1), Chen B(1).



Posterolateral tibial plateau fractures (PLTFs) are increasingly recognised in 
anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)-injured knees, yet their functional relevance 
remains unsettled. In our view, the recent study by Willinger et al. adds 
valuable prospective data on the association between PLTFs and lateral-sided 
soft-tissue pathology, but its findings should be interpreted with caution. The 
main concern is that PLTFs were analysed as a relatively uniform lesion despite 
substantial morphologic heterogeneity. Small cortical impressions are unlikely 
to have the same biomechanical significance as deeper depression defects 
associated with loss of submeniscal bony support or altered local slope 
geometry. In addition, preoperative pivot shift is an incomplete surrogate for 
the functional effect of PLTFs within a multifactorial instability pattern 
influenced by meniscal, anterolateral, and osseous restraints. The imaging 
framework also does not quantify structural variables likely to determine 
mechanical relevance. We therefore believe the study supports only a narrow 
conclusion: PLTF presence alone is not a reliable surrogate for greater 
preoperative pivot-shift laxity, whereas the significance of high-grade PLTF 
phenotypes remains unresolved.

title: The Deep Medial Collateral Ligament, Part 1: Quantitative, Qualitative, and Radiographic Anatomy.
authors: LaPrade RF, Wilebski BJ, Sawyer ER, Freetly TJ, Carlson MR, LaPrade CM, Tollefson LV, Retzer NK, Jelen PM, Super JT, Murray IR
abstract:
1. Am J Sports Med. 2026 Oct 26:3635465261492535. doi: 10.1177/03635465261492535.

The Deep Medial Collateral Ligament, Part 1: Quantitative, Qualitative, and 
Radiographic Anatomy.

LaPrade RF(1), Wilebski BJ(1), Sawyer ER(1), Freetly TJ(1), Carlson MR(2), 
LaPrade CM(1), Tollefson LV(1), Retzer NK(1), Jelen PM(1), Super JT(3), Murray 
IR(3).



BACKGROUND: The deep medial collateral ligament (dMCL) has historically been 
described as capsular thickening with meniscofemoral and meniscotibial 
components deep to the superficial medial collateral ligament (sMCL). However, 
recent investigations suggest that the dMCL includes capsular expansion beyond 
the traditionally described midthird ligament region.
PURPOSE: To define the attachment geometry and radiographic relationships of the 
dMCL using 3-dimensional coordinate mapping and standardized radiographic 
correlation.
STUDY DESIGN: Descriptive laboratory study.
METHODS: A total of 10 fresh-frozen cadaveric knees (mean age, 70.7 ± 6.8 years) 
were dissected to isolate the dMCL. A 6 degrees of freedom robotic testing 
apparatus with motion capture established 3-dimensional specimen-specific 
coordinate systems. The periphery of each femoral and tibial attachment site was 
digitized to determine attachment site geometry and spatial relationships to key 
medial landmarks. Radiopaque markers enabled standardized anteroposterior and 
lateral radiographic measurements.
RESULTS: Qualitatively, the dMCL demonstrated broad anteromedial capsular 
extension, with an anterior margin length of 27.0 ± 3.4 mm from the posterior 
aspect of the sMCL. Posteriorly, the dMCL blended with the anterior margin of 
the posterior oblique ligament. The femoral attachment was 10.7 ± 1.5 mm in 
anteroposterior width. The center of the femoral attachment of the dMCL was 
located 5.1 ± 2.0 mm posterior and 12.4 ± 3.5 mm distal to the medial epicondyle 
as well as 10.6 ± 3.2 mm distal to the center of the sMCL femoral attachment. 
The tibial attachment was 29.3 ± 3.7 mm in anteroposterior width and was located 
2.2 ± 0.8 mm distal to the joint line. Radiographically, the center of the dMCL 
femoral attachment was 7.9 ± 2.9 mm from the center of the sMCL femoral 
attachment. The tibial attachment center was 15.0 ± 3.6 mm proximal to the 
center of the proximal sMCL tibial attachment and 41.1 ± 5.3 mm proximal to the 
center of the proximal edge of the distal sMCL tibial attachment.
CONCLUSION: The dMCL demonstrated a broad and consistent anatomic footprint. 
Substantial anteromedial capsular expansion was consistently identified, 
extending anteriorly beyond the historically described narrow midthird capsular 
ligament deep to the sMCL.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings provide an updated qualitative and 
quantitative anatomic framework for future biomechanical investigations and 
should assist the surgical identification and radiographic assessment of the 
dMCL during medial-sided knee reconstruction procedures.

title: Calf Injuries: Anatomy, Pathology, and Treatment.
authors: Hauer TM, Arner JW, Mauro CS, Bradley JP
abstract:
1. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2026 Nov 1;34(21):e3032-e3040. doi: 
10.5435/JAAOS-D-25-01090. Epub 2026 Aug 6.

Calf Injuries: Anatomy, Pathology, and Treatment.

Hauer TM(1), Arner JW, Mauro CS, Bradley JP.



Calf injuries are common in athletes and typically result in missed time from 
sport and activities of daily living. The three individual triceps surae muscles 
can be injured, with differing described mechanisms. Gastrocnemius or plantaris 
strains tend to occur during sudden explosive movement of the ankle from a 
dorsiflexed to a plantarflexed position with the knee in extension. Soleus 
strains typically occur from repetitive dorsiflexion of the ankle with the knee 
flexed. Imaging modalities such as magnetic resonance imaging and 
ultrasonography can be helpful in determining the location and grade of injury, 
which can aid in treatment and return to play timelines. Classically, these 
injuries have been graded as grade I, II, or III, with grade I having <10% 
muscle fiber disruption, grade II having >10 to 50% muscle fiber disruption, and 
grade III having 50 to 100% muscle fiber disruption. The mainstay of treatment 
for most calf strains is nonsurgical, with surgical management being rare but 
reported in the literature for isolated grade III ruptures of the medial head of 
the gastrocnemius. Return to sport and activities requires a graduated physical 
therapy program focused on restoring tissue length without excessive strain. 
Recent limited evidence has shown promising results with quicker return to 
activities and decreased pain with platelet-rich plasma injections.

PURPOSE: To establish evidence-based consensus recommendations regarding the 
diagnosis and treatment of partial-thickness posterosuperior rotator cuff tears 
(PT-PS-RCTs). This part addresses the definition, classification, natural 
history and diagnosis of these controversial conditions in shoulder surgery.
METHODS: This official European Society of Sports Medicine, Knee Surgery and 
Arthroscopy-European Shoulder Associates (ESSKA-ESA) Formal Consensus was 
conducted according to the ESSKA Formal Consensus Methodology. A Steering Group 
developed 33 questions, followed by a standardized literature search and 
evidence review. For each question, a consensus statement was drafted and 
assigned recommendation grades (A-D) according to the level of evidence. An 
independent Rating Group evaluated all statements until strong agreement was 
achieved.
RESULTS: Twelve recommendations were generated with three Grade A, three Grade 
B, two Grade C, five Grade D and strong agreement. Grade A was found for the use 
of multiple classification systems in unison to characterize these injuries and 
for the distinction between acute and chronic tears. Scientific presumption 
level (Grade B) was found for the increased incidence of articular injuries in 
overhead and contact athletes and for the absence of a link between calcifying 
tendinitis and PT-PS-RCTs. Grade C was found to define the risk and timeframe of 
tear progression and the ideal imaging modality.

classified according to tear location, depth and tendon involvement. The 
aetiology of these injuries is multifactorial, and their progression is 
unpredictable. Current imaging modalities have limitations in characterizing 
these lesions. The present consensus provides clinicians with a practical 
evidence-based framework for the diagnosis and classification of PT-PS-RCTs 
while identifying key priorities for future clinical research.

title: Effects of fatigue are more pronounced on the uninjured side during single-limb jumps 2 years after an acute Achilles tendon rupture.
authors: Jónsdóttir US, Tranberg R, Silbernagel KG, Brorsson A, Briem K
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov;34(11):4187-4194. doi: 
10.1002/ksa.70579. Epub 2026 Aug 21.

Effects of fatigue are more pronounced on the uninjured side during single-limb 
jumps 2 years after an acute Achilles tendon rupture.

Jónsdóttir US(1), Tranberg R(1), Silbernagel KG(2), Brorsson A(1), Briem K(3).



PURPOSE: Achilles tendon rupture (ATR) is a serious lower limb injury that may 
result in persistent deficits in strength and endurance of the calf muscles. 
Compensatory mechanisms at proximal joints are known, but the effects of fatigue 
are less studied. The aim was therefore to evaluate the effect of a fatigue 
protocol on lower limb kinetics during performance of single-limb drop 
countermovement jumps (CMJ) in individuals with a history of a unilateral ATR.
METHODS: Thirty participants were recruited on average 2 years after ATR. Drop 
CMJs were performed on each side before and after a fatigue protocol, and peak 
power values for the hip, knee and ankle joints were calculated, as well as jump 
height and duration. A mixed model analysis of variance was used to evaluate 
inter-limb differences pre- and post-fatigue during the landing (eccentric) and 
push-off (concentric) phases of the involved (INV) and uninvolved (UNinv) side.
RESULTS: The fatigue protocol had a greater effect on peak ankle joint power of 
the UNinv side across both phases (by a mean [95% confidence interval, CI] of 
1.06 [0.58-1.54] W/kg) compared to the INV side (0.51 [0.03-1.00] W/kg; 
p = 0.039). Moreover, greater fatigue-induced changes in ankle joint power were 
found during landing (by a mean [95% CI] of 1.13 [0.64-1.61] W/kg) compared to 
push-off (0.45 [0.04-0.93] W/kg; p = 0.011), across both sides. A trend towards 
increased knee joint power was seen as a response to fatigue across both sides 
and phases (p = 0.062), with no change at the hip.
CONCLUSIONS: Rehabilitation following ATR should emphasize progressive reliance 
on the INV side across the rehabilitation continuum by incorporating strength, 
endurance and training under fatigued conditions. This approach may help reduce 
compensatory reliance on the UNinv side, potentially lowering the risk of 
overuse‑related injuries.

title: Four general-purpose large language models (ChatGPT-5, Claude 4, Grok 4 and Gemini 2.5) show comparable performance in specialised total knee arthroplasty clinical questions.
authors: Pujol O, Ferrer R, Coelho A, Oettl FC, Zsidai B, Leal-Blanquet J, Hirschmann MT, Samuelsson K
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov;34(11):4210-4218. doi: 
10.1002/ksa.70544. Epub 2026 Jul 23.

Four general-purpose large language models (ChatGPT-5, Claude 4, Grok 4 and 
Gemini 2.5) show comparable performance in specialised total knee arthroplasty 
clinical questions.

Pujol O(1)(2), Ferrer R(3), Coelho A(4), Oettl FC(5), Zsidai B(6)(7)(8), 
Leal-Blanquet J(2)(9), Hirschmann MT(10)(11), Samuelsson K(6)(7)(12).



PURPOSE: To evaluate and compare the performance of four general-purpose large 
language models (LLMs) (ChatGPT-5, Claude 4, Grok 4 and Gemini 2.5) in answering 
specialised clinical questions related to total knee arthroplasty (TKA) derived 
from the World Expert Meeting in Arthroplasty (WEMA).
METHODS: This is a cross-sectional comparative study. Twenty questions on TKA 
supported by moderate-strong level of evidence were randomly selected from the 
WEMA. Three orthopaedic surgeons independently performed a blinded assessment of 
all LLM-generated responses. An adapted version of the QUEST rating system, a 
comprehensive framework designed for the objective human assessment of LLM 
performance across healthcare-related subdomains, was used. Furthermore, the 
same three evaluators subjectively selected the best-performing LLM response for 
each question.
RESULTS: The four LLMs presented statistically significant differences in 
overall performance based on the QUEST framework (score range 1-5): Gemini 2.5; 
4.77 ± 0.06, Claude 4; 4.72 ± 0.07, ChatGPT-5; 4.70 ± 0.08 and GROK 4; 
4.62 ± 0.09 (p < 0.001). Gemini 2.5 achieved the highest scores in the Accuracy 
(4.58 ± 0.70), Comprehensiveness (4.87 ± 0.34) and Trust (4.52 ± 0.62) 
dimensions. However, Claude 4 obtained the highest score for the Currency 
(4.23 ± 0.67) dimension. When assessors subjectively selected the superior 
answer for each question, Claude 4 was chosen most frequently, in 46.7% of 
cases, followed by ChatGPT-5 in 25.4%, Gemini 2.5 in 22.9% and GROK 4 in 7.5% of 
cases.
CONCLUSIONS: Four general-purpose LLMs (ChatGPT-5, Claude 4, Grok 4 and Gemini 
2.5) demonstrated good overall performance when addressing specialised clinical 
questions related to TKA. No single model consistently outperformed the others 
across all evaluated domains.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level V.

title: Minimum joint space width demonstrates higher inter- and intra-observer reliability than Kellgren-Lawrence grading in knee osteoarthritis.
authors: Khela MS, Lee T, Mulford KL, Yang L, Brkljac M, Crossman D, Taunton MJ, Wyles CC
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov;34(11):4113-4124. doi: 
10.1002/ksa.70395. Epub 2026 Apr 14.

Minimum joint space width demonstrates higher inter- and intra-observer 
reliability than Kellgren-Lawrence grading in knee osteoarthritis.

Khela MS(1), Lee T(1), Mulford KL(1), Yang L(1), Brkljac M(1), Crossman D(1), 
Taunton MJ(1)(2), Wyles CC(1)(2).



PURPOSE: The purpose of this systematic review was to compare the inter- and 
intra-observer reliability of Kellgren-Lawrence (KL) grading versus minimum 
joint space width (mJSW) measurement on knee radiographs, and to examine the 
influence of rater type, radiographic view and atlas-based training.
METHODS: A systematic search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus and Web of 
Science was conducted through July 2025 following Preferred Reporting Items for 
Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Studies reporting 
inter- and/or intra-observer reliability for KL or mJSW on standard knee 
radiographs were included. Extracted data included kappa (κ) and intraclass 
correlation coefficient (ICC) values, rater expertise, radiographic view and 
atlas usage. Raters were categorized as expert, trainee/non-expert or artificial 
intelligence (AI)-assisted/automated.
RESULTS: Twenty-four studies (10,394 radiographs) met the inclusion criteria. 
Inter-observer reliability was generally higher for mJSW (mean 
ICC = 0.82 ± 0.17) compared with KL (mean k = 0.72 ± 0.17), with similar trends 
observed for intra-observer reliability. Experts and AI-assisted systems 
outperformed trainees/non-experts for both metrics. Reliability improved with 
semiflexed posteroanterior/Rosenberg views and atlas-guided training.
CONCLUSION: This systematic review demonstrates that mJSW measurement generally 
shows higher reproducibility than KL grading. Reliability improved with 
expertise, standardized imaging and structured training, and AI-assisted 
approaches performed comparably to expert raters. Quantitative mJSW should 
complement KL grading, particularly when combined with alignment measures, to 
enhance consistency and clinical relevance of radiographic assessment.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: No difference in patella mobility between conventional mechanically aligned and robotic-assisted functionally aligned total knee arthroplasty.
authors: Lachowski K, Naja KM, Prill R, Niemeier A, Salzmann M, Becker R
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov;34(11):4076-4081. doi: 
10.1002/ksa.70380. Epub 2026 Apr 9.

No difference in patella mobility between conventional mechanically aligned and 
robotic-assisted functionally aligned total knee arthroplasty.

Lachowski K(1), Naja KM(1), Prill R(1)(2), Niemeier A(3)(4), Salzmann M(1), 
Becker R(1)(2).



PURPOSE: Robotic-assisted (RA) surgery allows for higher accuracy in total knee 
arthroplasty (TKA) and for better standardization of alignment concepts. It was 
hypothesized that the more personalized component placement in functional 
robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty (RA-TKA) would show an impact on 
patella mobility and clinical outcome.
METHODS: Prospective study was performed on 80 patients who received TKA 
(Triathlon; Stryker). In 51 patients, the prosthesis was implanted using MAKO 
robotic assistance (RA-TKA), while 29 patients underwent conventional 
implantation (conventional total knee arthroplasty [C-TKA]). Patella mobility 
was compared pre- and postoperatively after three months. Medial and lateral 
translation was measured in extension by using a patellostabilometer (PSM), 
which measures medio-lateral patella mobility under a force of 10 N. Clinical 
assessment was based on Oxford Knee Score (OKS), Knee Society Score (KSS), 
Kujala and Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Arthritis Index (WOMAC) 
scores.
RESULTS: The medio-lateral patella mobility was 31 ± 9 mm before and 34 ± 7 mm 
(p < 0.01) after surgery. There was no significant difference in mediolateral 
patella mobility between the two groups (p = 0.282). Patella mobility increased 
by 3 mm in both groups after surgery. The medial and lateral shift ranged 
between 14 and 18 mm. All clinical scores (OKS, KSS, Kujala and WOMAC score) 
improved significantly from before to after surgery (p ≤ 0.001) without 
difference between the groups.
CONCLUSIONS: RA-TKA did not result in changes in patella mobility when compared 
to conventional implantation. Other factors, such as general joint laxity or 
implant design and component placement, may have a more significant impact on 
patella mobility and clinical outcome.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level II prospective designed study.

title: Patellar obliquity causes altered patellofemoral biomechanics in total knee replacement: An in vitro study.
authors: Shatrov J, Mounir Boudali A, Abe K, Parker D, Clarke E, Walter WL
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov;34(11):4010-4022. doi: 
10.1002/ksa.70201. Epub 2025 Dec 1.

Patellar obliquity causes altered patellofemoral biomechanics in total knee 
replacement: An in vitro study.

Shatrov J(1)(2), Mounir Boudali A(1), Abe K(1), Parker D(2)(3), Clarke E(1)(4), 
Walter WL(1)(3)(4).



PURPOSE: Patellofemoral joint (PFJ) complications are a common cause of 
dissatisfaction and revision after total knee arthroplasty (TKA). Asymmetric 
patellar resections may alter PFJ biomechanics. This study investigated the 
effects of patellar obliquity on PFJ kinematics and contact forces in a 
cadaveric model.
METHODS: Eleven fresh-frozen cadaveric knees (mean age 71.2 years) were 
resurfaced under three conditions: neutral thickness, medial-thick oblique 
(+2 mm) and lateral-thick oblique (+2 mm). A six-degree-of-freedom robotic 
system simulated passive flexion (0°-90°) and stair descent (10°-60°). 
Kinematics were measured with optical tracking; PFJ forces were recorded using a 
calibrated three-zone sensor (C1-C3). Kruskal-Wallis tests with 
Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc comparisons were applied (α = 0.05).
RESULTS: During passive flexion, medial-thick oblique produced greater 
medialization than native and lateral-thick (p = 0.013 and p = 0.009, 
respectively) and increased internal rotation versus native (p < 0.001). Central 
ridge pressure (C2) was higher in medial-thick versus lateral-thick 
(0.80 ± 0.54 V vs. 0.52 ± 0.44 V; p = 0.0189). Composite PFJ force (Newtons) did 
not differ between groups (p = 0.9126). During stair descent, medial-thick 
oblique showed greater medialization than native and lateral-thick (p = 0.017 
and p = 0.039) and increased internal rotation versus native (p < 0.001). C2 was 
higher in medial-thick than neutral (0.77 ± 0.49 V vs. 0.50 ± 0.49 V; 
p = 0.0106) and lateral-thick (0.45 ± 0.42 V; p = 0.0169). Composite force again 
showed no between-group difference (p = 0.3186).
CONCLUSION: Patellar obliquity alters PFJ tracking and regional loading-even 
without increasing total joint force-with a medial-thick oblique patella 
consistently elevating central ridge pressures. Prioritizing symmetric patellar 
resection may help avoid maltracking and focal overload that predispose to 
PFJ-related symptoms following TKA.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV controlled laboratory study.

Optimising methodology, biomechanics and imaging in biological augmentation for 
partial-thickness rotator cuff tears: A commentary on Demiral et al.

Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) combined with physical therapy (PT) represents a 
growing paradigm in the nonoperative management of partial-thickness rotator 
cuff tears (PTRCTs). In a recent publication in Knee Surgery, Sports 
Traumatology, Arthroscopy, Demiral et al. reported significant clinical and 
radiological improvements following PRP supplementation in articular-sided 
partial supraspinatus tears. While their findings provide encouragement for 
biologic augmentation, several methodological nuances warrant deeper 
examination. This commentary provides a broader critical perspective on three 
essential domains: baseline functional comparability and statistical model 
selection, the biological-biomechanical interface during early rehabilitation 
loading, and radiological precision in magnetic resonance arthrography (MRA) 
tear volume estimation. By addressing these methodological challenges, we aim to 
offer actionable guidance for future clinical trial designs and therapeutic 
protocols in sports medicine and orthopaedic rehabilitation. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE:

title: Clinical Outcomes of Arthroscopic Femoroacetabular Impingement Surgery for Adolescent Patients With Borderline Hip Dysplasia With a Minimum 5-Year Follow-up.
authors: Nishimura H, Afetse EK, Brown J, Felan NA, Garcia AR, Fukase N, Melugin H, Speshock A, Dornan GJ, Philippon MJ
abstract:
1. Am J Sports Med. 2026 Oct 26:3635465261491021. doi: 10.1177/03635465261491021.
 Online ahead of print.

Clinical Outcomes of Arthroscopic Femoroacetabular Impingement Surgery for 
Adolescent Patients With Borderline Hip Dysplasia With a Minimum 5-Year 
Follow-up.

Nishimura H(1), Afetse EK(1), Brown J(1), Felan NA(1), Garcia AR(1), Fukase 
N(1), Melugin H(1), Speshock A(1), Dornan GJ(1), Philippon MJ(1)(2).



BACKGROUND: The relationship between borderline developmental dysplasia of the 
hip (BDDH) and concomitant femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) has not been 
established in the adolescent population.
PURPOSE: To compare the minimum 5-year outcomes after primary hip arthroscopy in 
adolescent patients with BDDH and FAI to those with FAI alone.
STUDY DESIGN: Cohort study; Level of evidence, 3.
METHODS: A retrospective review of 122 adolescent patients who underwent primary 
hip arthroscopy for FAI by the senior author between February 2007 and December 
2016 was conducted. Eligible patients who were ≤19 years of age and whose 
proximal femoral physis had not yet closed and who completed a minimum 5-year 
follow-up were included. Then, patients with BDDH (lateral center-edge angle 
[LCEA], 18°-25°) were compared with patients without BDDH (LCEA, ≥25°). Outcome 
scores, including the modified Harris Hip Score (mHHS), Hip Outcome Score 
Activities of Daily Living (HOS-ADL), Hip Outcome Score Sport-Specific Subscale 
(HOS-Sport), Short Form-12 scores, and Western Ontario and McMaster Universities 
Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) score were prospectively collected.
RESULTS: In total, 23 patients with BDDH and 67 patients without BDDH were 
included. The mean follow-up times for those with and without BDDH were 6.60 
years (range, 5.24-9.73 years) and 8.17 years (range, 6.39-10.08 years), 
respectively (P = .063). After surgery, the BDDH group showed significantly 
lower mHHS (median, 96 vs 100; P = .027) and HOS-Sport (97 vs 100; P = .014) 
values and a higher WOMAC score (4 vs 2; P = .021) compared with the non-BDDH 
group. However, when looking at the percentage of patients achieving the minimal 
clinically important difference (MCID) and Patient Acceptable Symptom State 
(PASS) with mHHS, HOS-ADL, and HOS-Sport at 5 years, there were no significant 
differences between the 2 groups. Only 1 patient (4.3%) required revision hip 
arthroscopy in the BDDH group, while 8 patients (12%) in the non-BDDH group 
underwent revision hip arthroscopy. There were no cases that required conversion 
to periacetabular osteotomy.
CONCLUSION: Hip arthroscopy for FAI in growing adolescents with BDDH is safe and 
effective and yields equivalent achievement in PASS and MCID with clinical 
outcomes when compared to adolescents without BDDH.

title: Comparison of Costs and Postoperative Complications Between Carbon Fiber and Titanium Intramedullary Nails in the Treatment of Impending or Completed Pathologic Femoral Fractures: A Propensity-Matched Study.
authors: Rizk PA, Gonzalez MR, Morse AS, Lozano-Calderón SA
abstract:
1. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2026 Nov 1;34(21):e3159-e3167. doi: 
10.5435/JAAOS-D-25-01176. Epub 2026 May 18.

Comparison of Costs and Postoperative Complications Between Carbon Fiber and 
Titanium Intramedullary Nails in the Treatment of Impending or Completed 
Pathologic Femoral Fractures: A Propensity-Matched Study.

Rizk PA(1), Gonzalez MR, Morse AS, Lozano-Calderón SA.



AIMS: Despite the benefits of carbon fiber (CF) implants, concerns over their 
higher cost relative to titanium implants have limited their broader adoption in 
orthopaedic oncology. Our study compared the costs and postoperative 
complications associated with titanium and CF intramedullary nails (IMNs) in 
patients with femoral bone metastases.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective analysis of patients treated with titanium 
or CF IMNs for impending or completed pathologic femoral fractures due to 
metastatic bone disease between 2016 and 2023. Inpatient costs, 30-day costs, 
and 30-day postoperative complications were assessed. Mean and median total, 
direct, and indirect costs were evaluated using cost units. Propensity-score 
matching was conducted to minimize potential confounders.
RESULTS: After propensity-score matching, we included 91 and 45 patients treated 
with titanium and CF femur IMNs, respectively. No differences in age, sex, 
primary tumor, or comorbidity profile were found between groups. Mean and median 
total costs, direct costs, and indirect costs during the inpatient stay and at 
30 days postoperatively were similar between the titanium and CF groups. The 
mean length of stay was 8 days in both groups ( P = 0.70). Thirty-day 
complication rates were 25% and 20% in the titanium and CF group, respectively ( 
P = 0.50). No differences in 30-day readmission (25% in both; P = 0.35), 
mortality (4% versus 9%; P = 0.29), and revision surgery (1% versus 2%; P = 
0.61) rates were observed between the titanium and CF groups.
CONCLUSION: We found comparable inpatient costs, 30-day costs, and short-term 
postoperative complications between titanium and CF IMNs for impending or 
completed pathologic femoral fractures.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III.

title: Impact of Preoperative Heel Ulceration on Surgical Outcomes Following Open Reduction and Internal Fixation of Rotational Ankle Fractures.
authors: Tummala S, Wood BA, Wukich DK
abstract:
1. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2026 Nov 1;34(21):e3067-e3077. doi: 
10.5435/JAAOS-D-25-01184. Epub 2026 Apr 10.

Impact of Preoperative Heel Ulceration on Surgical Outcomes Following Open 
Reduction and Internal Fixation of Rotational Ankle Fractures.

Tummala S(1), Wood BA, Wukich DK.



BACKGROUND: As surgical treatment with open reduction and internal fixation 
(ORIF) becomes more common, attention to preoperative risk stratification has 
grown. Although multiple modifiable risk factors and comorbidities have been 
associated with adverse outcomes, the impact of preexisting decubitus heel 
ulcers in this context remains yet to be defined.
METHODS: Using a nationally representative multi-institutional database, a 
retrospective analysis was conducted on adults undergoing ORIF for rotational 
ankle fractures between 2010 and 2022. Patients with a documented decubitus heel 
ulcer within 4 weeks before surgery were compared with ulcer-free controls. 
After applying strict exclusion criteria and employing 1:1 propensity score 
matching for key demographic and clinical variables, 90-day medical 
complications and 1- and 3-year surgical outcomes were evaluated.
RESULTS: The presence of a preoperative heel ulcer was associated with markedly 
higher risks of 90-day surgical site infection, sepsis, pneumonia, urinary tract 
infection, mortality, and deep infection (all P < 0.005). At 1 and 3 years 
postoperatively, the ulcer cohort demonstrated markedly elevated rates of 
nonunion, revision surgery, and below-knee amputation (all P < 0.0125).
CONCLUSIONS: Preoperative decubitus heel ulceration is associated with elevated 
risks of both short-term complications and long-term surgical failure following 
ORIF for ankle fractures. These findings underscore the importance of thorough 
preoperative foot assessment and may inform surgical planning and perioperative 
management in this high-risk population.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Therapeutic Level III, Retrospective Cohort Study.
